articles.title_orig: Finnish Lawmakers Report Suspicious Home Break-Ins
articles.title_zh: Finnish Lawmakers Report Suspicious Home Break-Ins
articles.content_orig:
Police investigating reports of politicians’ homes being broken into in last year with nothing being stolen
The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, has said a foreign power could be responsible for a series of suspected break-ins at the homes of several members of parliament.
Police said on Thursday they were investigating multiple reports of MPs’ homes being broken into in the Helsinki area in the last year in which nothing was stolen but subtle signs of breaking and entering were left.
When asked by a reporter if a foreign power could be behind the alleged intrusions, Orpo said: “It is very possible. Quite possible in this day and age.
“If someone tries to destabilise Finland , our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity.”
He said the incidents would be investigated by police and within government and would be “taken very seriously”.
With the Finnish parliamentary elections just six months away, Orpo said the risk of election interference must be taken seriously. “We see in several European countries that Russia has sought to influence elections,” he said.
Finland shares a long border with Russia that has been closed for years amid a rapid deterioration of relations since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Finland joining Nato.
The Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, said when asked about the suspected incidents: “An attack on a member of parliament is an attack on democracy.
“It should not be allowed or accepted in any form … I stand in support of every member of parliament.”
At a press conference in parliament, the speaker, Jussi Halla-aho, said he did not have an exact number of suspected cases but that it was “significant”. He said it was the kind of behaviour associated with state actors.
“It is known that state actors sometimes engage in activities that resemble suspected cases, but we have no information to comment on at this time and there is no point in speculating,” Halla-aho said.
Observations had been made “drop by drop”, he said. “It is possible that the marks were left visible on purpose.”
According to the broadcaster Yle, suspected cases include doors being left open to homes and lights being left on.
Helsinki police said they had received information from parliament about suspected intrusions at the homes of MPs and had begun a preliminary inquiry. The force said in a statement: “The Helsinki police department is working closely with the national bureau of investigation in clarifying the matter. The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time.”

Alternative ways being used to move fuel out of Gulf region, but flows of refined products such as diesel still constrained
Exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.
Pipeline exports and ship-to-ship transfers are among the methods being used, according to analysts tracking the situation, while the US military continues to escort some vessels . However, flows of refined products such as diesel remain constrained, pushing prices higher.
At least 16.5m barrels per day (bpd) left the region in September, according to figures from the global trade intelligence firm Kpler, equalling the pre-war average, excluding Iran. The figure is 10.5m bpd higher than the monthly average for March, during the first weeks of the Iran war.
Since the conflict began on 28 February with US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran has sought to exert its authority on the strait of Hormuz and has at times even declared the strategic waterway closed .
However, Iran’s control appears to have declined in recent weeks, as oil exporters have found workarounds to address the disruption.
About 40% of the region’s crude is now transported without transiting the strait, compared with just 17% before the war, through Saudi and Emirati pipelines, according to Kpler analysis. Saudi Arabia was able to restart operations on its east-west pipeline in late September, after it was damaged during drone attacks , allowing exports from resume from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
In a sign of the other adaptations, the majority of crude transported through the strait of Hormuz is carried on a shuttle fleet mostly comprising very large crude carriers, sailing with their satellite transponders turned off. The cargo is moved on to different tankers in open water, usually off the coast of Oman or Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates .
More than 70% of the crude that passed through the strait in August changed tankers, whereas before the war almost no Gulf crude changed ships in the Gulf of Oman .
However, the recovery in exports from the region remains unbalanced, and supplies of refined products remain constrained.
This poses a problem for businesses and households that depend on refined products such as diesel to run their cars, vans and lorries.
The average diesel price in the UK hit an all-time high of 199.18p a litre on Monday, with many motorists already reporting prices above £2 on some forecourts.
“Diesel carries the sharpest risk,” said Kpler analysts, who found that less than 20% of pre-war levels of refined products shipped through Hormuz were being transported.

They recorded a seven-day average of 677,000 bpd of refined products as of Monday, compared with 3.6m before the conflict.
Even as oil exports from the region have increased, the level of threat to ships operating around the strait of Hormuz has not disappeared.
“New routes emerge, cargos are rerouted, risk is priced in and absorbed. The danger is assuming that resilience equals security. It doesn’t,” said Richard Meade, the editor in chief of shipping publication Lloyd’s List. “Oil flows have recovered because the market participants have accepted greater operational complexity and higher costs. The underlying threat remains.”
The danger to vessels and their crew was highlighted on Tuesday, when three Liberian-flagged tankers were hit by projectiles while transiting the strait.
The price of crude remains at elevated levels and moved higher again on Thursday, as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.
The price of Brent crude briefly was back above $100 a barrel on Thursday, up 3% to $101.
The rise came after reports that China had suspended exports of oil products to regions beyond Hong Kong and Macau, a move that would add further pressure to oil markets. Oil analysts said China’s decision could suggest it was concerned about the availability of domestic products.

articles.title_zh: Israel's Netanyahu: Co-pilot of flydubai plane underwent radical Islamist indoctrination
articles.content_orig:
Israel could respond if investigators confirm an Iranian link to the co-pilot accused of trying to crash the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight, regional sources told Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst.
Reporting on “America Reports,” Yingst said the investigation remained ongoing after President Donald Trump suggested Iran may be connected to the suspect.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cautioned that it was “too early to say whether he had any connections with Iran or with anyone else.”
Fox News contributor and Hudson Institute senior fellow Rebeccah Heinrichs said a weakened Iranian regime could still inspire or direct violence, while the segment emphasized that no connection had been established.
Heinrichs also praised the passengers and wounded captain who intervened, comparing their courage to Todd Beamer’s actions aboard United Flight 93.
“It’s that kind of courage and behavior that’s really going to save the day,” she said.
She warned against allowing the attack to undermine progress between Israel and the UAE, calling flydubai a symbol of the Abraham Accords.
The airline has suspended flights to and from Israel while authorities investigate.
Airlines need to look harder at the people inside the cockpit, an aviation security expert warned after the attack aboard the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight.
Arik Arad, founder of CYVIATION and former head of security for El Al at Ben Gurion Airport, said the incident should prompt stronger employee screening and closer attention to pilots’ mental health.
“I don't think that most of the airlines are actually aware of a potential threat that comes from the inside the cockpit,” Arad said.
He recommended psychological, behavioral and environmental assessments alongside pilots’ required medical exams and simulator training to identify stress or other problems.
Airlines, he argued, may be unwilling or unable to devote enough resources to monitoring pilots’ daily mental health.
Arad predicted the incident would lead to additional security procedures and regulations, including changes to employee background checks.
“I believe this will teach us all a lesson of how to actually examine pilots further,” he said.
Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo praised Israeli passengers who intervened aboard the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight, saying their heroism helped avert a catastrophe.
“The attempted terrorist attack aboard the FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv could have been absolutely catastrophic, if not for the heroism of the Israeli passengers on board,” Pompeo wrote on X.
While acknowledging that details were still emerging, Pompeo delivered a forceful message of support for Israel.
“The people of Israel will never be defeated by jihadism,” he wrote. “Never forget that their fight is our fight too.”
In a separate post, Pompeo also praised Capt. Smit Machchhar, the wounded pilot credited with opening the cockpit door so passengers and crew could intervene.
Pompeo said everyone should aspire to the captain’s bravery and quick thinking, adding, “Praying for his quick recovery.”
The captain and co-pilot involved in the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight incident have left Saudi Arabia for Abu Dhabi accompanied by an Emirati security team, Saudi Arabia’s Interior Ministry said Thursday.
Both had been hospitalized and were cleared to travel after their conditions improved, according to a translation of the ministry’s statement.
The ministry described preliminary findings as an “altercation” between the captain and co-pilot that injured both. Its statement did not address Israeli officials’ allegations that the co-pilot attacked the captain and tried to crash the aircraft.
Saudi authorities said the plane landed safely in Tabuk at 9:45 a.m. Wednesday with 174 passengers and eight crew members aboard.
Passengers continued their journey on a replacement FlyDubai aircraft at 5:40 p.m. The remaining crew returned to Dubai separately.
The ministry said Saudi investigators worked with a UAE security team and emphasized that its response followed international and humanitarian obligations.
An Israeli father who helped subdue the accused attacker aboard the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight said his three young daughters screamed that they did not want to die as the aircraft plunged.
Passenger Tzvika Manes told Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst that his daughters, ages 11, 7 and 6, were terrified during the cockpit attack.
“They were shouting, ‘We don't want to die,’” Manes said, describing “very emotional and very traumatic moments.”
Manes was one of four Israeli passengers who helped overpower the co-pilot accused of attacking the captain, Yingst reported from Tel Aviv.
“When your family is behind, you're running to the fire,” Manes said. “We're trying to save them.”
He recalled passengers shouting and falling under the forces of the aircraft’s dive.
“He tried to do 9/11 in Israel,” Manes said. “And thank God we overcome this situation.”
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the suspect appeared to have been radicalized but cautioned that possible connections remained under investigation.
“I think it's too early to say whether he had any connections with Iran or with anyone else,” Netanyahu said in remarks aired during the report.
President Donald Trump told reporters Thursday that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) "could have been" responsible for the bloody attack on FlyDubai flight 1073 on Wednesday.
When asked by Fox News' Peter Doocy if he had been briefed on a possible connection between Iran and the Omani copilot who stabbed the FlyDubai pilot, Trump responded, "We're working on it. Right now they're being very open with us. I would say the answer based on what I'm hearing is yes."
Trump also, in response to Doocy asking if the attacker could have been trained by the IRGC, said "could have been."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox & Friends on Thursday morning that it was too early to know if the attacker had terrorist connections, but said we would know soon.
An Israeli mother and her two children described the traumatic experience of witnessing blood and screams during Wednesday’s attempted hijacking of FlyDubai flight 1073 in a Thursday interview with Fox News’ Harris Faulkner.
“What can I say, it was a horrifying situation, it felt like forever,” Lital Shahar recalled.
Lital, who was interviewed alongside her 14-year-old daughter Hila and 11-year-old daughter Eliya, explained that she had both girls and their two other sisters, ages 7 and 5, on the flight.
Lital said they were “really traumatized from what happened.”
“I was experiencing a lot of fear because I didn’t really understand what was happening,” 11-year-old Eliya told Faulkner. “I was going through lots of thoughts of hope, getting back home, and another thought of being like ‘I don’t want to die.’
“There was a lot of screams, a lot of blood, a lot of things that [made me] wish I wouldn’t go on the flight,” Eliya added.
Lital described the exact moment she found out something was wrong.
“Suddenly there was a woman, [who] came out of business class and started screaming. There was lots of blood. ‘He stabbed him, he stabbed him!’” Lital recounted the woman shouting.
“The Israeli men, the heroes that were on the plane, jumped into action,” she continued. “Yaniv, the one that everyone is saying now and talking about, was sitting a row behind me, and was so quick I didn’t even see him.
“I just saw him coming back after everything kind of finished, full with blood on his clothes. And the other men were in the first rows so I didn’t see them as well. They were really heroic. And Captain Smith was able, in his last powers, to open the door of the cockpit that saved us all. We are so grateful for him as well,” Lital added.
The mother of four said the situation was not only a miracle, but a culmination of multiple miracles.
“In that moment we realized, I realized, that we are in the hands of God, and he’s the only one who can save us now.

articles.content_orig:
Fiona Lowe, the daughter of actor Chad Lowe and producer Kim Painter, has died, the family announced.
“We are deeply heartbroken by the loss of our beloved Fiona,” the Lowe family said in a statement posted Wednesday to the Instagram stories of her sister, Mabel Lowe.
The family remembered Fiona as “a loving young girl who was smart, creative, and loved to dance.”
The statement added: “She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents. In fact, she was the light of our lives.”
“Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time,” the family statement said. “If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988.”
Fiona Lowe’s cause of death was not announced. People was the first outlet to obtain the family statement.
Her grandfather, Chuck Lowe, said Wednesday on Instagram : “Rest in peace sweet Fiona.”
Born on Nov. 16, 2012, Fiona Lowe was the second of Chad Lowe and Kim Painter’s three daughters.
Chad Lowe, an Emmy winning actor with television roles on “Life Goes On” and “ER” who is the brother of actor Rob Lowe, often posted photos of his children on his Instagram page. That included shots of the whole family, pictures of the three girls together and video clips that show the family enjoying their travels and day to day lives.
One of his most recent posts of Fiona Lowe featured her on her 13th birthday.
“Celebrating Fiona officially becoming a teen today!!” Chad Lowe wrote in the caption. “Keep dancing through life FiBear! Love you soooo much!!”
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or chat live at 988lifeline.org . You can also visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional support.
Rebecca Cohen is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft makes Windows settings backup the default in 26H2
articles.title_zh: Microsoft makes Windows settings backup the default in 26H2
articles.content_orig:
Annual update installed. You're up to date, so nothing seems to have changed. Wait a minute...
Windows 11 26H2 is out, and Microsoft has enabled Windows settings backup by default, a move that could send administrators scrambling to opt out where they once had to opt in.
The latest release hasn't made a lot of shockwaves in the community featurewise. Users with up-to-date versions of 25H2 will unlikely notice much difference – 26H2 has the same code base, delivered via an enablement package. It even has the same set of known issues, although all are now "mitigated" in one way or another.
However, administrators will spot several important changes. The end-of-support clock is reset, and Microsoft has flipped some switches behind the scenes; notably, enabling Windows backup and restore (formerly Windows Backup for Organizations) by default.
The service, which was previously off by default, backs up a device's settings and a list of installed Microsoft Store apps. The idea is that when a user moves to a new device, a restore can happen during setup. Microsoft also listed an objective of the service as allowing "organizations to transition to a cloud-first approach for managing devices and user settings."
The problem is that many organizations are prohibited from sending this data to the cloud. As a result, the default-on setting won't apply in privacy-sensitive regions such as those covered by the EU Digital Markets Act, or in sovereign and restricted environments.
For many others running Windows 11 26H2, it'll now be enabled by default on eligible devices – Entra joined or Entra Hybrid joined. Unless an administrator has explicitly said no to the functionality, the act of installing the update will flip the switch, and the backups will begin.
Administrators will rightly be wary of anything that switches from opt-in to opt-out, even something so apparently useful and innocuous as a backup. Why wouldn't you want your users to be able to leap to a new device with ease? That assumes their data is also in the cloud, of course, since this only backs up settings and a list of Windows apps. Backing up data is something else entirely.
That is the real issue with the change. The release of Windows 11 26H2 isn't particularly exciting in itself, but flipping a long-standing opt-in to opt-out as part of it is likely to set more than a few nerves jangling. ®

articles.title_orig: Trump’s AI rebrand may stop at the White House
articles.title_zh: Trump’s AI rebrand may stop at the White House
articles.content_orig:
When President Donald Trump gathered execs from the world's most powerful tech companies in the White House on Tuesday to discuss the future of artificial intelligence, one company was conspicuously absent: Apple .
Neither Chairman Tim Cook nor his successor as CEO, John Ternus, were present, while leaders from every other tech megacap – and many other companies – lunched with Trump.
Apple didn't respond to CNBC's questions about the meeting, nor did the White House.
Social media buzzed with conjecture that Apple wasn't invited because the company is behind on AI.
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, a powerhouse investor in Silicon Valley and a Trump ally in the second term, called Apple's absence a " nothing burger " in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday.
"I can assure you, they're very much read in on all of this, and I suspect they agree with all of it," Gerstner said.
Cook, as Apple's public face with government officials around the world, was at the White House less than a week ago, when he attended Trump's state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Gerstner pointed out.
Cook stepped down as Apple CEO in September, handing the baton to hardware specialist Ternus.
As part of the transition, Apple noted that Cook would still handle "engaging with policymakers around the world" as the company's executive chairman. His new role was underscored last week at the state dinner with Xi.
Over the years, Cook has put in the time to maintain a good relationship with Trump. He's made over 10 public appearances at events in the president's second term, including Trump's inauguration, in the oval office, at Davos, and at state dinners on multiple continents. He attended the "Melania" screening at the White House.
Throughout his dealings with Trump over the past two years, Cook has stayed on message, focused on Apple's manufacturing interests and trade issues, at a time where its products could be subject to tariffs . The company has given the Trump administration wins on issues like American investment and jobs while trying to ward off Trump's longstanding desire for the company to make iPhones in the U.S.
More recently, Apple has reportedly sought to use Chinese-made memory chips as prices skyrocket around the world, but doing so requires a license. Commerce Secretary Lutnick said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal that "the Trump administration is not in favor of that."
Gerstner, in his CNBC interview, said that the participants at the lunch were the companies that were "really pushing the frontier on model development."
The iPhone makers' in-house models are smaller and more efficient than the so-called "frontier" models developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, which were both represented. Apple Foundation Models are mostly designed to run on Apple's own silicon inside iPhones and Mac computers. They run parts of Siri, while OpenAI and Anthropic's models use massive Nvidia -based clusters of chips.
Apple is a consumer company, whereas most of the frontier lab AI competition happens in the enterprise. Apple partners with Google to develop its models. Its capital expenditures are tiny compared to the sums Google, Microsoft , Meta , and Amazon are investing.
While some investors fret that Apple is falling behind in AI, the market has increasingly seen it as a hedge to other capex-heavy tech names. And the company just launched a new AI-powered Siri earlier to mostly positive reviews.
Apple's stock is up 22.5% so far in 2026, outpacing the Nasdaq and almost all of its megacap peers other than Nvidia, which is up about the same amount.
Though Apple is very much touting the power of AI and its role in the technology's future, company executives have been mostly absent from the public debate around AI safety or alignment, which were primary topics at Trump's luncheon.
Nobody at Apple has penned the long manifestos like the ones coming from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft and others.
As part of Tuesday's meeting with Trump, the White House and the leading AI companies signed an accord, committing the industry players to various safety measures. After the meeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI COO Greg Brockman, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei all signed the document.
Cook has said several times over the years that Apple is more likely to weigh in publicly on policy that "intersects with our company in some way." Apple's not dealing with alignment issues on the frontier.
"If it doesn't intersect — if it's something where we would just be another voice out there and not have a unique perspective to bring — then we don't say anything," Cook said in a 2021 DealBook interview.

articles.title_orig: General Motor Q3 sales drop 5.5%, while Toyota buoyed by EVs, hybrids
articles.title_zh: General Motor Q3 sales drop 5.5%, while Toyota buoyed by EVs, hybrids
articles.content_orig:
General Motors on Thursday reported a year-over-year sales decline of 5.5%, with 670,974 new vehicles sold during the third quarter.
GM's sales of all-electric vehicles are down across the board, as enthusiasm for EVs wanes. EV demand spiked last year ahead of the Trump administration ending up to $7,500 in federal incentives for consumers to purchase an electric vehicle. During the same period last year, GM reported record sales of its electric vehicles.
Against those comparisons, EVs this year saw dramatic drops, with the Equinox EV down 92.4% during the most recent quarter, at 1,905 vehicles sold. The Blazer EV was down 84.4% and Hummer EV sales fell 72.9%.
The report comes after Cox Automotive said last week that new vehicle sales have been stronger than expected this year and raised its 2026 forecast by roughly 2%, to 16.1 million units.
Hybrid vehicle sales are expected to capture a growing market share of car sales, as inflated gas prices pressure consumers.
Despite offering a broad EV lineup, the Detroit automaker only offers one hybrid vehicle, a Corvette. Experts expect GM's weakness in the sector to impact its overall sales.
Hybrids assisted other automakers in outperforming GM in third-quarter sales.
Toyota Motor reported that its EV and hybrid vehicles made up over 57% of the Japanese automaker's sales this quarter.
Toyota said sales were up 0.6% for the most recent quarter, with 633,223 vehicles sold. Sales of its electrified vehicles, which include hybrids, were up 28.5%, with 363,367 units sold.
That helped Toyota continue to narrow its gap with U.S. sales leader GM, which is now less than 136,000 units. That compares to a full-year gap of roughly 335,000 units last year.
Cox Automotive earlier this year said if such sales trends continue, Toyota could once again overtake GM to become the U.S. sales leader in the coming years.
Honda Motor, which also offers several hybrids and leads major automakers in fuel economy in the U.S., reported a 9.3% increase in U.S. third-quarter sales. Its hybrid sales were a record of more than 106,000 units during the quarter.
"We've got really high demand for hybrids," Lance Woelfer, head of American Honda Motor's U.S. sales, told CNBC. "We're finding more and more consumers are figuring out hybrids meet their needs."
High fuel prices, with an AAA national average of $4.41, were also expected to impact sales of big trucks and SUVs, sectors that GM relies on. GM's full-size pickups were relatively flat.
Each of the automaker's brands are down so far year to date, led by a 25% decline in Cadillac.
GM's lower-cost vehicles are a bright spot for the company as consumers face high inflation. The Chevrolet Trailblazer was up 51% for the third quarter, while sales of Buick Envista were up 18.4% and Chevrolet Trax up 16.3%.
Despite falling sales, Duncan Aldred, president of GM North American, remained optimistic.
"Our business is performing very well, the launch of our next-generation full-size pickup trucks is on track, and we are making investments in new vehicles, innovative technologies, and our U.S. manufacturing footprint to drive our next phase of growth," Aldred said in a statement .
General Motors last month announced additional details about its new V-8 engines for its pickup trucks, as it attempts to maintain leadership in truck sales.

articles.title_zh: South Korea Contests U.S. Claims of New $50 Billion Alaska Investment
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's $200 billion investment into the U.S., which President Donald Trump said would transform America "for generations," is not a done deal in totality.
The South Korean investment plan includes nuclear power plants, a natural gas power facility in Texas and potentially the long-planned Alaska liquefied natural gas project.
Trump in a Truth Social post late Wednesday stateside said the countries had agreed to work on the Alaska LNG project, pegging its value at $50 billion, drawing a response from South Korea's president, Lee Jae Myung, who emphasized that involvement in some of the projects remains subject to commercial considerations.
Lee in an X post on Thursday local time said that participation in the Alaska LNG project was dependent on its financial viability and legal compliance. He added that investments in nuclear power plants would also require assessment of commercial viability on a plant-by-plant basis.
Trump had hailed South Korean investments in his post late Wednesday stateside, saying that the countries had agreed to work on the Alaska LNG project, pegging its value at $50 billion.
The joint statement earlier Wednesday, however, had mentioned that work on the project was contingent on "commercial reasonableness," without highlighting details on allocations toward the project.
The Alaska LNG project seeks to transport natural gas roughly 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) from fields on Alaska's North Slope to the southern part of the state, where it would be liquefied for export to markets including Asia, reported Yonhap. The project has faced long-standing questions over its economics given the large up-front investment required.
Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan had described it as "high-risk" last year and said participation would be difficult unless it could generate sufficient cash flow.
Overall, the investment package includes $22.3 billion for a 6,472-megawatt natural gas power facility in Encinal, Texas, that will supply electricity to co-located data centers. The project will be led by developer Related Cos. and U.S. power company NextEra Energy , with the first phase expected to begin commercial operations in 2029 and the full facility coming online in stages by 2032.
Trump said the investments would turn South Korea's commitments into "huge construction projects" and create "tens of thousands of American jobs."
"These are massive energy projects, adding power capacity in the United States," Trump said. "This is new construction, new manufacturing, and great jobs for American workers."
The two countries said they would seek to expand Korean companies' participation in the Texas project across equipment supply, engineering and construction as well as long-term operations and maintenance. The U.S. also intends to give Korean companies opportunities to supply equipment, including turbines, to similar projects in the country.
Another $120 billion has been allocated to plans for eight large-scale nuclear reactors in the U.S. Of that amount, $100 billion is earmarked for construction costs and $20 billion for contingency reserves.
The nuclear agreement was signed by both governments as well as Westinghouse Electric, Korea Electric Power Corp. and Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power. The plan also calls for pursuing a potential significant minority investment in Westinghouse by Korean companies, with the terms subject to commercial negotiations.

articles.title_orig: ‘She was pure love’: Renee Good’s partner makes first public comments as family sues U.S. government, ICE officer over her killing
articles.title_zh: ‘She was pure love’: Renee Good’s partner makes first public comments as family sues U.S. government, ICE officer over her killing
articles.content_orig:
The partner of Renee Good, a Minneapolis woman who was fatally shot by an immigration officer in January , spoke publicly about her death for the first time Thursday as the family announced that they have filed two federal civil lawsuits.
“She was pure love, and she was funny, and she was smart, and she was gorgeous,” Becca Good said at a press conference, becoming emotional as she discussed attending back-to-school night and preparing to celebrate Halloween with their children alone.
“Every single one of these moments for all of her babies and for everyone up here was a monumental moment, and she should be here for all of them. We were all robbed,” she said.
Earlier in the press conference, attorneys for Renee Good’s family announced lawsuits alleging wrongful death and excessive force in her Jan. 7 death.
One lawsuit seeks to hold the United States liable under the Federal Tort Claims Act for the actions of federal agents. It alleges wrongful death, battery, assault, false imprisonment, emotional distress and negligence.
The second suit names Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot Good, as well as several federal officials, including White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.
“Every morning she’s my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama, and how I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” Becca Good said.
Renee Good’s brother, Brent Ganger, said her death was “completely senseless.”
“We file these two lawsuits today to put officials on notice that we have not forgotten,” he said.
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A representative for Ross could not immediately be identified.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the office will “vigorously defend” the claims in the lawsuits. Bis also shared a statement from President Donald Trump, who said Good’s “actions were pretty tough.”
“When you look at the way that car was pulled away… there are a couple versions of that tape that are very very bad,” Trump said.
Good, 37, was fatally shot in the driver’s seat of her SUV during a Jan. 7 encounter with Ross. The killing occurred about a month after the Trump administration deployed 3,000 immigration agents to the Twin Cities in what officials have dubbed Operation Metro Surge. Agents descended on Minnesota after right-wing influencers drew attention to a state fraud scandal involving Somali nationals.
The operation triggered massive protests and significant pushback from state leaders. It ended in February .
The shooting was captured on cellphone video. It showed Good’s partner, Becca Good , standing outside the SUV calling Ross “big boy” and telling him to remove the covering from his face. Other officers at the scene could be heard telling Good to get out of the car. In the video, Good is seen turning the steering wheel away from Ross and beginning to drive.
Multiple gunshots can be heard in the video before Good’s SUV crashes into a parked car. In a separate video recorded by Ross, a male voice could be heard saying “f-----g b----” moments before the crash.
Trump administration figures, including President Donald Trump and Noem, defended Ross’ actions and claimed Good was an agitator who tried to run over the officer with her vehicle. Witnesses told NBC News at the time that Ross didn’t appear to be in the direct path of the SUV.
Noem said Ross was treated at a hospital for injuries he sustained in the incident and was released soon after. A DHS official previously told NBC News that Ross sustained internal bleeding but did not elaborate on his injuries.
Attorney Antonio M. Romanucci, who is representing Good’s family, said he hopes the lawsuits “are the beginning of the ultimate legal weapon in uncovering the truth behind this unlawful use of deadly force and the nefarious conspiracies behind the invasion of American cities by American law enforcement officers.”
Weeks after Good’s killing, Customs and Border Protection agents shot and killed Alex Pretti , a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, in Minneapolis.
Minyvonne Burke is a senior breaking news reporter for NBC News.

Public frustration over the economy and rising prices is weighing heavily on President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections, with a majority of Americans blaming his policies for stubbornly high costs.
Just 17% of US adults approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living, while 26% approve of his management of the broader economy, according to a new Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
Nearly two-thirds, 65%, say Trump's policies are primarily responsible for high prices rather than factors outside his control, amid frustration over tariffs and the war with Iran.
The findings come weeks before midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Trump has been campaigning heavily for Republicans, but dissatisfaction has spread to some of his own supporters.
"I was hoping it would be better or different, but it’s not really good," said Robert Gault, 66, a retired factory worker and Republican from Bradford, Pennsylvania.
"He said, ‘Make America Great Again.’ And I have not seen him do that."
Concern about everyday expenses has risen sharply. About half of Americans say they are "extremely" or "very" concerned about affording gasoline, up from 39% in July, while a similar share are highly concerned about food costs.
"Just the cost of everything is going up as a result of fuel," said Pedro Sanchez, 52, a California law enforcement worker who voted for Trump. "I used to have a lot more disposable income. I don’t have that any more."
Trump's economic approval has fallen 14 percentage points since March 2025. About 7 in 10 Americans say his handling of living costs has been worse than expected, including roughly half of Republicans.
About 6 in 10 Republicans now disapprove of Trump's handling of living expenses, up from about half in April, although 67% of Republicans still blame high costs primarily on factors outside his control.
The poll also found growing dissatisfaction with Trump's foreign and trade policies. Some 69% of Americans say the war with Iran has not been worth fighting, while just 28% approve of Trump's handling of Iran.
Only about 3 in 10 approve of his handling of international trade, and 64% say he has gone too far with new tariffs.
Overall, about 3 in 10 Americans approve of Trump's performance as president, while roughly 6 in 10 say the country is worse off than when his second term began. Border security remains his strongest issue, with about half approving of his performance.
Trump's economic approval is now comparable to President Joe Biden's 28% rating in June 2022 during pandemic-era inflation. But Americans were less likely to directly blame Biden at the time: in October 2022, 44% said his policies were responsible for high prices, compared with 65% who now blame Trump's policies.
Sanchez said Trump's tariffs and the Iran war had directly contributed to his disappointment.
"I think he has a lot to do with it," he said. "I think with Biden, a lot of the stuff was outside of his control."

Going into Micron's ( MU ) Q4 earnings on Wednesday, analysts weren't too concerned about demand for the company's memory and storage.
After all, data center builders are buying up chips so fast that Micron and rivals SK Hynix ( SKHY ) and Samsung ( 005930.KS ) can't keep up.
But Wall Street watchers did have their eyes on the company's gross margins, which have continued to climb throughout the AI explosion .
"Can gross margins stay up at the rates that they are, or do we need to see some normalization so it doesn't feel like, you know, price gouging in a moment?" Creative Strategies CEO and principal analyst Ben Bajarin said to Yahoo Finance ahead of Micron's earnings announcement (video above).
During the company's earnings call, Micron CFO Mark Murphy explained that he anticipates Q1 gross margins will set a new floor and that they'll climb higher from there.
Analysts have also been on the lookout for more information about Micron's strategic customer agreements (SCAs), long-term arrangements that lock in the lowest possible price for memory and storage chips.
According to Murphy, Micron's Q1 margins will take a ding due to increased fiscal 2026 financial compensation related to manufacturing. The company absorbed most of that increase in Q4, but the impact will be felt in Q1.
As a result, he told analysts, Micron anticipates gross margins will climb beyond Q1 on the back of more moderate price increases.
Micron stock is up around 280% this year as of Tuesday's close.
SCAs are meant to serve as a hedge against a downturn in future memory sales. Outside the AI boom, the memory and storage industry traditionally experiences boom-and-bust cycles. SCAs are designed to protect against a quick decline in sales while providing the company with a clearer understanding of future revenue.
According to CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, Micron has signed 26 SCAs, which the company estimates will account for over 35% of its revenue through 2030.

articles.title_orig: Mike Tomlin spent 12 years building a Minecraft city. Over 19 minutes, he showed it off to the world
articles.title_zh: Mike Tomlin spent 12 years building a Minecraft city. Over 19 minutes, he showed it off to the world
articles.content_orig:
The former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach took 12 years to build a city filled with stadiums, skyscrapers and bespoke homes. It is a marvel
We may finally have cracked the case as to why the Pittsburgh Steelers stagnated so much over the final years of Mike Tomlin’s tenure as head coach: he was focused on virtual urban planning.
I’m kidding, of course. It’s good when people in high-pressure jobs have creative hobbies. Count this writer (and his interior designer wife) among those who were gobsmacked on Wednesday night by Tomlin’s reveal of a 12-year-long project in Minecraft, the world-building game. Tomlin had teased that during his coaching career, he took up Minecraft city-building as a way to connect with his young children. We have now seen the fruits of that labor, and they are magnificent . Look my my works, Terry Bradshaw, and despair.
“More than anything, it was therapeutic for me,” Tomlin says at the video’s outset. One can see how this sort of “mindless entertainment” would’ve been helpful to a man in his position. Tomlin was building up his Minecraft city (whose name is still unclear) during a tumultuous period in Steelers history. When star tailback Le’Veon Bell declined to sign his franchise tag in 2018, keeping the Steelers offense in limbo all season? Tomlin had Minecrafting. When Antonio Brown blew up his relationship with Ben Roethlisberger and ultimately forced a trade to the Raiders? Tomlin had Minecrafting. When the Pittsburgh sports media turned on him for not winning any playoff games in nearly a decade? Minecrafting, still.
Where Tomlin’s description of his Minecraft experience doesn’t make sense, however, is when he calls the experience “mindless”. It’s clear that Tomlin’s project was anything but.
The city is built around a central body of water, not terribly unlike the city where the coach built his NFL legend. (Pittsburgh has three rivers meeting at Point State Park. Tomlin’s city has a big lake from which the whole urban landscape flows outward.) “This is kind of where it all started, around this body of water,” the coach deadpans. “I thought it was appropriate to just give you that perspective of where I wanted to get started from.” He sounds like he’s about to read off his team’s Week 4 injury report, but no. Tomlin is about to take us through his universe, one he crafted over the years with evidently painstaking detail.
Tomlin tells us about the first building he ever constructed, ostensibly around 2014, when the Steelers won the AFC North behind a 1,700-yard receiving season from Brown and 1,300 on the ground from Bell. It’s a “boutique hotel” with an executive spa off the main lobby, featuring therapy rooms. He takes us into a multipurpose conference room on the other side, with tall windows and a glass roof.
“I was very lighting conscious,” Tomlin tells us. “You’ll consciously see me do things with glass ceilings where appropriate.”
We see more and more as Tomlin flies us around. He breezes right past a virtual CVS and into an aquarium-themed apartment highrise. “I did it because it was across the street from the aquarium that I built in the city,” he explains, in case anyone thought the water features were out of place. Tomlin promises that we will see the aquarium in a future episode and that it will be “crazy”. His son and producer Dino, a former college wide receiver, tells us that it took a lot of time for his dad to get the water all situated.
“That was a nightmare,” Mike says.
It goes on and on. Tomlin explains that he was “fixated” on providing details in bedrooms. He is also conscious that not everyone in his city will be an NFL fan: Tomlin built an MLS stadium as well as a baseball field that fits neatly into the cityscape, not terribly unlike Pittsburgh’s PNC Park. He relishes in the fact that one of his highrises has a good view of the ballpark. Tomlin tells us that he is “view-conscious”, and indeed, the man seems to take a special pleasure in a city vista.
The finer details are not left to chance, either. In office and multipurpose space, we learn of the coach’s passion for providing an “appropriate number of public restrooms.” Tomlin built his city with the well-roundedness of a good gameplan, understanding that a successful operation means not just acquiring glitzy wide receivers (or swanky apartment complexes) but also good linemen (toilets).
We also see touches of Tomlin’s family life. He built a collegiate apartment complex called “The View”, which shares the name with a particularly grungy complex in College Park, Maryland, where Dino began his college career. (Your correspondent had many long nights in the same complex, one he hopes to never revisit for the rest of his life.) We get the sense that there will be much more to see.
In some dark corners of the internet, Tomlin’s hobby was met with condescension.
“There is a tension between trying to appreciate people’s widely diverse passions, and the feeling that some people are wasting all of their ambition and energy,” tweeted one person with the job title “chief economist”. It was a bizarre sentiment about a man who won a Super Bowl and became one of the most decorated coaches in the history of the NFL before going on to a lucrative career in broadcasting.
Fortunately, it was also a minority view. The overarching response to Tomlin’s Minecraft build could only be described as adulation. People found it refreshing that a 54-year-old with one of the most high-profile, pressurized jobs in the US would develop a personal hobby that bakes in as much creativity and thoughtfulness as this one. The city of Pittsburgh should hire Tomlin as a planning consultant.

articles.content_orig:
If you’re lucky, you’ll watch one TV show a year that changes you forever. Take my word for it: Netflix ’s East of Eden is that show, whether or not you’ve read John Steinbeck’s seminal 1952 novel, East of Eden . By the end of its seven episodes, timshel —a Hebrew word that Steinbeck reinterpreted to mean “thou mayest,” and arguably serves as the lifeblood of the story—is something you’ll want to tattoo on your psyche, so that you may never forget your capacity for change.
If you consider East of Eden ’s place in American literature, it’s almost shocking that something as sweeping as Netflix’s adaptation—which far surpasses the scope of the 1955 film (famous for James Dean’s breakout vehicle) and towers above the well-regarded, but little-seen 1981 miniseries—hadn’t existed until now. This East of Eden comes from creator Zoe Kazan, the granddaughter of Elia Kazan, who directed the 1955 film. (Which was nominated for four Academy Awards, but only covers the latter third of the novel.) Her deep love of a story that clearly shaped her childhood imagination is clear, but she doesn’t let reverence get in the way. Her secret? Clearly, casting four actors at the absolute zenith of their powers: Florence Pugh, Christopher Abbott, Mike Faist, and a breakout Hoon Lee.
A well-paired Abbott and Faist play Adam and Charles Trask, respectively, as quarreling brothers who grow up as farmers on the East Coast. A mysterious young woman named Cathy (Pugh) shows up on their doorstep, bloodied, and eventually marries Adam. She gives birth to twins (later played as teenagers by Joseph Zada and Joe Anders), while Charles plays homewrecker. Then, Adam and Cathy move to the Salinas Valley in California, where they meet a friendly neighbor in Samuel Hamilton (a wizened Ciarán Hinds) and hire a servant, Lee (Hoon Lee).
Throughout most of the series, Kazan foregrounds Cathy, of whom Steinbeck wrote in the novel: “It doesn’t matter that Cathy was what I would have called a monster. Perhaps we can’t understand Cathy, but on the other hand we are capable of many things in all directions, of great virtues and great sins.” Thanks to career-best work from Pugh, Kazan brings us as close as we’ll ever come to understanding Cathy. Her performance is at different times violent, distant, and tragic, mostly in her scenes away from the claustrophobic Trask households. Abbott, meanwhile, is a perfect match: Often with just a few words or even a look, he unfurls a wounded man whose welts and bruises make it such that he’ll never understand her.
To fully explore every one of Kazan’s decisions in her adaptation—including the unfortunate but necessary decision to background the Hamilton family (save  Samuel)—would spoil the lost-in-a-good-book feeling the series will give you. But it’s worth noting the turn-of-the-century costuming, which is masterful but never attention-grabbing, from the Trask family’s button-ups to the lace dresses at Cathy’s brothel. And though Kazan shot East of Eden in New Zealand, her framing of the Salinas Valley is like a classic landscape painting: amber, grass, dawn, dusk. It’s Steinbeck’s words come to life.
Most of East of Eden ’s reviews, justifiably, praise Pugh’s powerhouse turn as Cathy as East of Eden ’s greatest coup. But it’d be an Adam and Eve-level sin to say that this adaptation simply does not punch this hard without Hoon Lee, a longtime theater and TV player (most recently in Apple TV’s Your Friends and Neighbors ) who we should immediately consider as one of our greatest working character actors. Steinbeck’s depiction of Lee is surprisingly modern, showing a man facing prejudice in mid-twentieth-century America, code-switching between cultures, but daring to dream of the life he deserves. Hoon Lee runs with what’s in the text and deepens the man considerably, adding a fateful trip to San Francisco that’s much shorter in the novel. Lee’s performance is tender, heartbreaking, and radically optimistic, the human embodiment of timshel .
East of Eden , famously, is an Adam and Eve tale, wrestling nature against nurture, and whether we really, truly, can break the cycle we were born into. It’s not just biblical in the literal sense, but it’s a Bible for how to live a life. In a time when so many people, myself included, feel powerless against every damn thing we’ve faced these past few years, Kazan’s vision of timshel isn’t just revolutionary. Thou mayest . It’s a rallying cry. And it just might change your life.

articles.title_orig: What a Pearly King taught me about Cockney rhyming slang and East London history
articles.title_zh: What a Pearly King taught me about Cockney rhyming slang and East London history
articles.content_orig:
George Major, known as the Pearly King of Peckham, wears his blinged-out suit in 2024. He died in August at age 88. Tony Kershaw/Getty Images hide caption
LONDON — He was one of my most memorable interviews. Even though we were both speaking English, I could barely understand a word he was saying.
"The costermongers, wheeze used to fly-pitch, on this frog and toad," he said — at least I think, after listening to my tape several times again, none the wiser.
Our interview was back in 2016, on one of my first NPR reporting trips to London. George Major, then 78, was a local celebrity. We walked together through the East End, where the factories and docklands that Major grew up around during World War II have given way to glass skyscrapers. A vendor ran out into the street to slap him high-five. Tourists snapped photos.
Major had turned up in bling: A black suit and flat cap, both festooned with sequins, sparkles and mother-of-pearl buttons. His title — Pearly King of Peckham — was spelled out in shimmering buttons across the back of his jacket.
He was a charming wheeler-dealer. But his language — a mix of what he called "backspeak" and Cockney rhyming slang — was impossible for this hapless American visitor to understand.
At one point in our video interview, I glanced at the camera and exclaimed, "We might need a translator here!"
Ten years later, I chuckle whenever I land at Heathrow Airport, where a portrait of Major covers an entire wall. But this summer, a former colleague alerted me to an item in the local press, which hit me harder than I expected: The Pearly King of Peckham died Aug. 1, aged 88.
He was buried Sept. 14 in a cemetery not far from the Cockney Museum he founded. A horse-drawn cart carried his casket into a little chapel, whose walls shook with mourners singing raucous pub songs. One of the gardeners outside looked bewildered.
At the gravesite, I approached the Major family, offered condolences, and hesitantly shared the story of my brief, confusing 2016 encounter with their loved one.
A horde of pearly kings, queens, princes and princesses — four generations of Major's family, all in matching pearly suits — turned and looked at me, some through tears, then threw back their heads and laughed.
"A real Cockney cheeky chappy!" his daughter Janet Major said, hugging me.
Pearly kings and queens, wearing clothes decorated with mother-of-pearl buttons, are committed to raising money for charities. Laura Chiesa/LightRocket viz Getty Images hide caption
In the 1870s, an orphaned street sweeper named Henry Croft began decorating his suit with mother-of-pearl buttons scavenged from the streets outside textile factories that used to dot London's East End.
His pearly garb infused menial work with dignity — a royal air, even — and launched what would become a working-class East London institution: The pearly kings and queens .
"These pearly suits are now cultural artifacts with fantastic designs, telling a profound story about London and Cockneys, what we call the non-posh Londoners," says Andy Green, co-founder of the Modern Cockney Festival, an annual celebration of diverse, working-class communities in London.
Some of the so-called pearlies were street hawkers, market vendors or fly-pitchers — unlicensed traders. Others canvassed for charity. Many were immigrants, their slang peppered with words from Yiddish or Bengali. They became neighborhood fixtures, in mother-of-pearl finery.
"You had what are called costermongers, which is a posh word for street hawkers, street sellers," Green says. "Imagine you're a newly arrived immigrant in the country. One of the first jobs you could possibly do might be to hustle, sell goods on the street."
That's what George Major did. Born in 1938 inside a military barracks in Peckham, southeast London, he was abandoned as a child, grew up in a workhouse , and found odd jobs in the local market as a teenager, his daughter Janet explains.
"Dad eventually became one of the costermonger kings that used to run market stalls," she says. "It was not an easy childhood, but he followed the ideals of Henry Croft. That was before the welfare state, when you had to help your friends, your neighbors, your community."
Janet Major describes the weekends of her childhood, with her father leading all seven of his children, walking door to door in matching pearly suits, asking for money for charity.
Nowadays, a dwindling number of pearlies still canvass for charities like children's hospitals, women's shelters and veterans groups. They appear at summertime street festivals and march in parades.
George Major later trained as a plumber and ran a plumbing supply shop, she says.
Onscreen, the pearly kings inspired the streetwise, heart-of-gold chimney sweep character of Bert in Walt Disney's Mary Poppins film — played by Dick Van Dyke, an American who later owned up to what he called "the most atrocious Cockney accent in the history of cinema."
The Major family and others believe George Major himself inspired another fictional character: Del Boy , the happy-go-lucky East London huckster in the long-running British sitcom Only Fools and Horses . He's a cheeky salesman, always scheming to get rich quick, with the catchphrase, "This time next year, we'll be millionaires!"
At his funeral, Major's eulogy was riddled with Del Boy quotes.
But like the TV protagonist, Major also broke the law. In 2012 he was sentenced to six months in prison, after pleading guilty to benefits fraud . He was released early.
"If he could avoid the tax man, he would!" his daughter laughs. "He used to say, 'Discount for cash!' He'd love a bargain."
His fame overshadowed his legal troubles. Major was one of dozens of pearly royals who marched in the opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics.
George Major, seen here in 1975, was born in 1938 inside a military barracks in Peckham, southeast London, and grew up in a workhouse before he became the best-known pearly king of his generation. Chris Moorhouss/Hulton Archive via Getty Images hide caption
Years later, I finally figured out what Major meant back in 2016 when he told me he was a "costermonger" (street hawker) who used to "fly-pitch" (sell stuff without a license) on the "frog and toad" where we did our interview.
In Cockney rhyming slang, "frog and toad" means road. "Porky pies" means lies. "Apples and pears" means stairs. "Whistle and flute" means suit. "Ruby Murray" means curry. The vocabulary is extensive, and bewildering to outsiders — which is precisely the point. Green, the Cockney expert, says this type of slang likely originated as a code to confuse the police, or to secretly rig prices among street vendors.
To complicate things, Major also spoke in what he called "backspeak," sometimes also called backslang, which is even more confusing. One example that's crept into mainstream British slang is the word "yob" for boy. Take any word at all, and simply spell it backwards.
One of the only parts of that 2016 interview I could understand at the time was when Major waxed poetic about his family's unique pearly suit pattern. He pointed to a row of buttons on his sleeve, calling them "the line of life."
Ten years later, at his funeral, I found myself examining the same pattern on a pearly outfit worn by his great-granddaughter.
"There's a straight line, which is your life line," Aleisha Gordon, 19, said, pointing to a row of shimmering buttons. "The triangles are the ups and downs in life, and the flowers are the friends and family that help you along the way."
After the funeral, children threw handfuls of earth as George Major's coffin was lowered into the ground. The undertaker brought out four caged doves for Major's descendants to release skyward. The birds circled twice overhead, then disappeared.
People shared anecdotes about a "real rascal" and "the most hilarious person" who was nevertheless "very particular" about who made his tea. Someone turned on a boombox, and mourners began kicking their legs

articles.title_orig: Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
articles.title_zh: Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
articles.content_orig:
Adam Polovincik on the Flydubai flight
A man has described how he hugged and reassured his two young children as their plane suddenly descended after one pilot stabbed the other in an attempt to seize control of the flight.
A Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes around two hours into its journey from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered him and retook control to land safely.
Adam Polovincik told BBC Newshour that he hugged his six-year-old son and three-year-old daughter "really hard" and tried to stay calm for them as the attack unfolded.
He praised the pilot who was stabbed and passengers who fought off and subdued the attacker, saying they were "true heroes".
The stabbed pilot is in a stable condition in hospital, while the alleged attacker has been arrested.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to say whether Iran was involved in the attack , but that the alleged attacker had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
Polovincik, who was sitting in aisle 13, was flying home with his wife and children after an "amazing" holiday in Singapore and Thailand.
He said there had been a "huge degree of panic" on the plane as there was a "very, very, very sharp decrease in height".
What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel
He thought at first that this was simply because of an air pocket, but "it took a lot of time, almost a minute".
Everyone who had not been seated fell to the floor, the 40-year-old said.
"After a couple of seconds, we started to hear screams. 'There is blood, there is stabbing, we need help'," Polovincik said.
"At the end of the day, you understand very, very quickly that literally there is nothing that you can do at this point in time," he said.
Polovincik, a performance marketing analyst, said he tried to "be cool" for his children.
"You just tell them, yeah, everything's going to be all right. It's just a malfunction in the aeroplane, there is a crew under control, the passengers are helping them, [you] hug them really hard and try to keep your face so it doesn't look very panicked, try to keep your tone of voice."
But he said there was naturally a "high degree of panic" on the flight.
There were lots of families with children on the plane because the flight took place towards the end of a Jewish holiday period.
After about 10 to 15 minutes, he said a passenger in the cockpit told them the incident was "under control" and other staff were flying the plane.
In a video released by Netanyahu's office, passenger Yaniv Hayun described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him out of the cockpit before other passengers helped pin him down.
Two other pilots who were onboard the flight then took over the controls and safely landed the plane, which had been carrying more than 150 passengers.
Polovincik said: "After they told us that the situation is, again, 'under control', then it was a bit harder to tell the kids that it's malfunctioned because people start to walk around the aeroplane covered with blood."
Polovincik was praised Indian pilot, Capt Smit Machchhar, who fought off his attacker and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing passengers to step in.
"Without him opening the door, we're probably not speaking here right now," he said, adding that he "can't even start saying our gratitude for this human being".
Polovincik said that, although he was not religious, he could not escape "the feeling that it was the hand of God yesterday" that had put "the pieces on the board in the way that they did".
After the situation onboard was brought under control, the flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where Polovincik stressed the passengers, who were almost all Israeli, were treated well.
"They brought us water and food and coffee and even sweets for the kids - even though we don't have any diplomatic relationship between Israel and Saudi Arabia," he said.
The alleged attacker, who was arrested in Saudi Arabia, is expected to be transferred to the United Arab Emirates, from where the plane departed, Netanyahu told Fox News.
The passengers were taken to Tel Aviv on another flight later on Wednesday and were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.
Polovincik said it had been "such a terrible ending" to an amazing family trip and that it would take some time for his family to come to terms with what had occurred.

articles.title_zh: Pete Hegseth’s War Daddy-sermon about killing and Jesus was truly eye-opening
articles.content_orig:

L ast year, self-proclaimed lethal war enthusiast and committed Christian Pete Hegseth gathered all the generals in the US military — forcing some to fly from as far afield as South Korea — to call them fat and shout about how much he hates DEI.
Beards were out, “war fighters” were in, AMERICA WAS BACK (to getting itself entrenched into forever wars in the Middle East) and Hegseth got to preen around talking about strength and integrity and all those other things he wouldn’t know if he bumped into them in a dark alley. It was a heck of a speech.
Today, dear reader, he gathered the generals again for another announcement. And he took last year’s teachings even further.
There was, of course, the standard opener about “reviving the warrior ethos,” about making the US military “the most capable, the most focused and the most lethal,” and how “telling someone to lose weight” is “not discrimination, that’s leadership.” There was a truly excellent aside about how there would be no more “drag queen shows,” which made the military under Biden sound a lot more fun than I had presumed. And there was also an incredible claim that there will be “no more gender pronouns,” which is going to make basic communication quite difficult, but screw it: let’s commit to the bit. No more adjectives! NO MORE VERBS! NO MORE GODDAMNED BASIC GRAMMAR! Let’s take this all the way, boys!
We were treated to Hegseth’s meme-tastic little slogan, exhaustively designed to offend: “No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps and no radicals.” And then we were told that the “delusional media” and “fake news,” which is run by “anti-American losers” and “haters,” is worse than Iranian state propaganda.
“A free press, of course, is important,” he added — deliberately drawing out the word ‘important’ in a sardonic way that seemed to imply he meant simply important in theory — but unfortunately the free press today is “fundamentally anti-American. It’s sick. It’s a national betrayal. It’s treason, actually.”
Here was classic Hegsethean nuance. And look, all of this is obviously fascist-adjacent and weird, but it’s also what you expect from a speech by Pete. What you only sometimes get is a spiral into bizarre religious fervor, and it turned out that that was what was coming today.
“Jesus said do unto others as you have done to yourself,” Hegseth continued, and that is the reason why he is making every unit in the War Department (a Jesus-like name change if ever there was one) into a platoon he would be happy to send his own children to join. Would Jesus send his children to do lethal war-fighting in this platoon?! If the answer is “not just no, the answer is hell no” then something is wrong. And to be fair, when Jesus is involved, isn’t the answer always “hell no”?
As part of this Jesus-like improvements of units, Hegseth has also done away with psychological testing because, the War-not-Defense Secretary claimed, those tests were all just there to get more Black women into the army or something. Instead, they’ll now have a “merit-based assessment” on how to “win on the battlefield,” because screw checking whether or not these kids are psychologically stable before we hand them AR-15’s.
This kind of woke bureaucratic nightmare of psych testing, Hegseth continued, standing in front of a huge digital overlay of an American flag, only happens when your department is being run by “strong patriots and not weak weirdos.” Thank goodness we now have a man who has never once projected ‘weak weirdo’ energy in charge, eh?
There was a further announcement about the military being open for business with “the new, nimble” startups funded by people like Steve Feinberg, “a patriotic billionaire” (and is there any other kind of billionaire?) This will lead to “drone warfare supercharged by SI-enabled functioning,” so essentially killer bots, which by the way won’t be restrained by any “red tape” so they’ll be coming real soon. The term “autonomous war fighters” was thrown around a lot, which isn’t exactly reassuring.
But don’t worry! Hegseth has also announced today that he is launching Project Meridian, an effort led by America’s three “best minds”: Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey, and 83-year-old Newt Gingrich. The room was, of course, military-silent when he said this — one presumes any room would be — so he then had to ask everyone to stand up and applaud. Clap, assorted non-fat, non-woke generals! Clap for the superior intellect of Newt Gingrich!
We will put our lives in the hands of “President Trump, a man that understands leading from the front and also from the edge,” Hegseth added. But wait, what? Which edge? Don’t worry about it, because Hegseth was back on his religiosity kick: he’s bringing Christianity back to killing, he said, because we need fewer “anti-American, DEI-worshipping woke factories” like liberal arts colleges with their “Che Guevara and critical theory,” and we need more students who understand Rome, Philadelphia and Jesus (these were his actual examples.)
So chaplains and churches and “religious support” will become a new priority. No more “political correctness and secular humanism” (perish the thought!) Instead, there will be an Office of Religious Affairs that “will report straight to the top”. (By the top, he means himself, by the way, not to God, and like all Christian groups, “it’s gonna have real teeth”.)
Hegseth then quoted Psalm 33:12, “Blessed is the nation whose god is the Lord. That line of the Bible is specifically referring to Israel, but sure.
“While we wage physical war,” he continued, “we know the real fight is spiritual.” The Book of Isaiah, he said, sees God asking Isaiah who he can send in his name, and Isaiah responding, “Send me.” Hegseth then extended this verse to suggest that Isaiah might also say: “Send me to fight the communists. Send me to fight the Islamists,” before concluding to the generals that “lethality is your calling card and victory your only acceptable end-state.”
What is actually said in the Book of Isaiah is instructive, as the biblical writer in question suggests during these verses that if people are “always hearing, but never understanding” and “ever seeing, but never perceiving,” with “hearts that are calloused,” then they will never truly “see with their eyes,” “hear with their ears,” “understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed.”
Oof, how inconvenient for War Daddy Pete! But it doesn’t matter because, as Hegseth rounded off his speech, “We are the War Department and we never back down.” Not in the face of logic, not in the face of real quotes from the Bible, not in the face of people trying to give us college educations!
And then he stalked offstage after giving a couple of stony-faced thumbs-up, ready to lead us all into a bold future. Godspeed, brave companions! And boy oh boy, isn’t Jesus going to be ecstatic that he’s coming back to the US military just in time for the AI-powered killer bots?!

articles.title_orig: Statement Written by Police in Cornell Assault Case Omitted Her Claim She Was Raped
articles.title_zh: Statement Written by Police in Cornell Assault Case Omitted Her Claim She Was Raped
articles.content_orig:
A woman who accused seven members of a fraternity at Cornell University in 2024 of rape reportedly told the school's investigators that she "felt like bait" on the night of the alleged assault.
"I felt like lions around me," she said during a 2025 hearing, according to ABC News . "It just was a totally debilitating place to be in."
The comments were included in a 99-page report prepared by the university as part of its Title IX investigation, per ABC.
The report also included comments from a fraternity member who Cornell's investigation concluded did not engage in the assault but was found responsible for "attempted sexual exploitation."
"I was sorry that maybe if it wasn't consensual and she was victimized, I was sorry for not stopping it," the fraternity members said, according to ABC.
In a civil lawsuit filed last month against the school and the fraternity members, the woman, a former student identified as "Jane Doe," said that she was the victim of a "gang rape" at the Chi Phi fraternity on Cornell's Ithaca, N.Y., campus on Oct. 19, 2024. She said she was already intoxicated when she arrived and was given ketamine before and during the alleged assault. She reported the incident to campus police three weeks later.
On Tuesday, CBS New York published excerpts from a Nov. 14, 2024, interview with police, in which she asserted, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
Cornell University Police vehicles are seen on campus on Sept. 29.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, the New York state prosecutor who reopened a criminal investigation into the case, said he was not provided with a transcript of her interview with campus police before his office decided not to pursue charges.
"I'm going to follow up on this because this is news to me," Van Houten told the network. "If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more. Like I said, that wasn't provided to me."
In a lengthy statement released on Monday, Van Houten announced that he had started pursuing criminal charges against the seven fraternity members and would present the case to a grand jury. He also sought to explain why he initially decided not to prosecute them.
According to Van Houten, Jane Doe "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped" in a six-page sworn statement to campus police in November 2024.
"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual," Van Houten said. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later."
It's unclear exactly when the sworn statement cited by Van Houten was given. He did not immediately return a request for comment.
Cornell University issued a statement on Monday saying it supported the district attorney's decision to reopen the case while pushing back against claims that the school did not thoroughly punish those involved in the alleged assault.
"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," the university said. "A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced on Wednesday that Cornell has agreed to initiate an independent review of its initial response to the allegations a day after the governor had called for one.
"I spoke with Cornell's president today, and the university has agreed to bring in outside counsel for an independent investigation," Hochul wrote in a post on X . "I've directed my team to look at what more we can do to strengthen protections for survivors. This culture has to stop. And in New York, we're going to do everything we can to stop it."
The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., is seen on Sept. 28.
On Sept. 14, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell University and seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, alleging that she was the victim of a "gang rape" at the fraternity house when she was incapable of consent — and that the school failed to protect her from "sexual predators" on its campus.
The defendants named in the lawsuit include Cornell, the seven fraternity members, the Chi Phi fraternity, the woman's own sorority, Delta Delta Delta, and an off-campus bar that allegedly served her alcohol.
She is seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages resulting from "sustained psychological injuries, severe emotional distress, along with pain and suffering and loss of enjoyment of life."
According to her lawsuit, Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the school in October 2024 when she went to visit a friend at the fraternity house on Cornell's Ithaca, N.Y., campus while intoxicated. Shortly after arriving, Jane Doe alleged that she was pressured by two fraternity brothers into snorting what they said was ketamine before sexually assaulting her. One of the men then allegedly sent a message to the fraternity's Snapchat group suggesting that she was available for sex. A screengrab of part of the chat was included in the lawsuit.
According to the complaint, multiple other members of the fraternity showed up, and she was raped for hours.
"The Snapchat was disgusting and vulgar and immoral," Van Houten told ABC News. "But the question that we analyzed was, did Jane Doe consent to what happened? And the law in New York state is clear: That if you are voluntarily intoxicated, or under the influence of drugs such that your judgment is impaired, that does not legally under the penal law constitute your inability to consent."
During the alleged assault, the fraternity members "began pouring lines of Ketamine all over her body and snorting them," according to the complaint.
"At around 5:45 AM, this assault concluded and Plaintiff lost consciousness," the lawsuit stated.
About three weeks later, on Nov. 8, 2024, Jane Doe reported the incident to the university's police department.
According to ABC News , Jane Doe told police in a sworn statement on Nov. 15, 2024, that the incident "felt like coercion," and that at one point she said "no to the foursome" one of the fraternity brothers had proposed. She also stated: "I felt like I was unable to make any decision because of how intoxicated I was."
According to the New York Times , she told Cornell's Title IX investigators that she did not consider herself a victim until she saw the incident being discussed in an online forum.
"Are Chi Phi brothers Crips or Bloods because I hear they have been doing hell Gang Banging?" one user wrote.
"They do drugs and gang r*ped a sophomore," wrote another.
"That's the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn't a whore and that I was assaulted," Jane Doe told investigators, per the Times.
A student walks past a Cornell University sign in Ithaca, N.Y., on Sept. 28.
Cornell's months-long Title IX investigation included at least 12 hearings, according to the lawsuit, which said that the accused fraternity members were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell."
Two of the seven accused fraternity members were ultimately expelled, while the others received lesser sanctions, according to the complaint. Jane Doe dropped out of school.
Last week, Cornell issued a statement saying that it had concluded its Title IX investigation but would not disclose individual sanctions, citing federal privacy laws.
"The Cornell Office of Civil Rights and the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies.
