articles.content_orig:
President Trump has said the kingdom of Saudi Arabia "wouldn't be here right now" if it wasn't for him, while reiterating the same claim about Israel.
In an interview with TIME magazine published Thursday, the president was asked about his relationship with Saudi Arabia, after CBS News and other outlets reported that he had turned down a request from the kingdom to join Saudi forces in bombing the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
"Good," Mr. Trump said of his ties with Saudi leaders. "I've done a lot for Saudi Arabia. I protect Saudi Arabia. If I weren't president, Saudi Arabia wouldn't be here right now. Neither would Israel. They'd be wiped off the face of the planet."
"I like the crown prince," he added, referring to Mohammed Bin Salman. "My relationship is very good. But remember, if I weren't here, there wouldn't be a Saudi Arabia. There wouldn't be an Israel. There wouldn't be various other countries, also."
President Trump has acknowledged that the U.S. has limited supplies of some munitions, but he called a recent Pentagon report about munitions shortages caused by the Iran war, "mostly fake news."
"Some forms of ammunition are a little bit lower than other forms," the president said in an interview with TIME magazine published Thursday, adding: "We're stocking up at levels we've never done before."
Mr. Trump's comments were published two weeks after the U.S. Department of Defense's inspector general said in a report that "the munitions expenditure on [Operation Epic Fury in Iran] has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply."
Mr. Trump called the report "mostly fake news," and said the cost of restocking U.S. weapons would be, "less than we make in Venezuela for one month."
Iran's Mission to the United Nations in New York said its delegation left the city on Monday evening as scheduled, rejecting reports that it had been asked by the United States to leave.
The mission said the departure had been planned in advance and that the schedule had been communicated to the U.S. Department of State on Sept. 17.
Axios reported Wednesday that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had asked the delegation on Monday to leave New York after negotiations between the two nations , carried out via mediators, stalled, citing a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter.
"Having achieved nothing, the State Department has resorted to propagating baseless and worthless news," Iran's mission said in a post on X about the reported request from Rubio.

"Passengers whose final destination is Tel Aviv will not be accepted for travel at the point of origin," said the UAE government-owned airline in a statement Thursday , adding that "customers already en route to Tel Aviv will be accommodated and provided with all possible support to complete their journeys."
FlyDubai flights from Tel Aviv have been suspended amid investigations into the alleged attempt on Wednesday by a FlyDubai co-pilot to crash a plane carrying more than 170 people, most of them Israelis, after stabbing the captain.
Passengers were able to subdue the attacker, believed to be an Omani national, and the plane made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Passenger Ron Levi told CBS News on Wednesday "it was the most frightening experience we've ever had in our lives."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said the co-pilot underwent "Islamist radical indoctrination," but he told CBS News on Wednesday that it was "too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here. I think we'll find out, won't take a long time."

Netanyahu, speaking to Fox News late Wednesday, said Israel had given Britain information about a plot shortly before Burnham's government, on Sept. 8, joined 11 other nations in announcing sanctions on products from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

"We gave the Brits the intel that there was going to be an attack, and it's an Iranian-sponsored attack. And pretty much the next day, they slapped sanctions on us."
President Trump earlier spoke of a possible Iranian role in the incident near the British base, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that it " clearly involved" a foreign actor, without offering any evidence.
The nature of the incident remains unclear, and police have said no viable explosives or weapons were discovered. The men, who arrived in a rural village near the base in the dead of night in three vehicles, had large plastic drums, many appearing empty from aerial video, and a quantity of gasoline.
According to British media, one of the five men called the police himself about an hour before they were reported by a resident. Police said Monday that the men could have been, "either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."

The number of people applying for US unemployment benefits dipped last week to the lowest level since mid-July as lay-offs remain low and most American workers enjoy job security.
The Labor Department said on Thursday that initial jobless claims ticked down to 197,000 from a revised 198,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, dropped by 2,500 to 200,000.
Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for lay-offs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. So far this year, claims have mostly stayed below 220,000 – historically low.
The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher energy prices that have squeezed businesses and consumers since the fighting with Iran began February 28.

articles.content_orig:
Rapper Rick Ross was arrested Thursday in connection with a domestic violence incident at his Star Island mansion, where a woman accused him of repeatedly striking her and restricting her breathing during an altercation in August, according to Miami Beach police.
Ross, whose legal name is William Leonard Roberts II, voluntarily surrendered to detectives at Miami Beach Police headquarters Thursday before being taken into custody, police said. He was booked into the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center at 6:10 a.m.
The 50-year-old rapper faces one felony count of battery by strangulation and one misdemeanor count of battery. According to Miami Beach police and the arrest affidavit, the charges stem from an alleged late August domestic violence incident at his residence on Star Island that was reported to police on Sept. 29.
The arrest affidavit says Ross and the alleged victim had been in a relationship for about a year and were living together at the time of the alleged incident.
The woman told investigators that on Aug. 28 she was awakened around 7:44 a.m. by Ross, who she said was angry because she had been tagged in a photo on Instagram. Police said Ross questioned her about whether she was lying to him and allegedly slapped her in the face.
Later that morning, according to the affidavit, Ross accused the woman of being involved with another person and continued questioning her while she was in a bathroom. The woman told police Ross struck her in the chest several times and restricted her breathing by grabbing and twisting the collar of the hoodie she was wearing.
The affidavit alleges Ross then grabbed the woman by her ponytail and slammed her against a wall before striking her in the face, causing a busted lip. The report states he then pushed her to the floor, turned on the shower and attempted to spray her with the shower head. The woman was eventually able to leave the bathroom and later gathered her belongings and left the residence after Ross left, according to the affidavit.
Police said the woman later provided detectives with a sworn statement and timestamped photographs of her injuries. Investigators also reviewed surveillance video from the residence that they said showed a friend arriving to pick her up and being turned away. According to the affidavit, Ross later posted a photo on his Instagram account showing the friend arriving at the property.
Ross denied the allegations in a video statement posted to his Instagram Stories around noon Thursday.
"First and foremost, I'm totally innocent of the fabricated allegations made against myself. I repeat, I am totally innocent with these fabricated allegations," Ross said. "I have such an amazing team, and I'm totally confident that these fabricated allegations will be laid to rest."
Earlier on Thursday, Ross' attorney, Bradley Horenstein, also denied the allegations against his client and urged the public not to rush to judgment as the case moves through the legal process.
"All I can say is that the allegations are false. He's innocent. Everything is going to come out," Horenstein told CBS News Miami. "We just ask that you allow the process to play out before rushing to judgment, because the truth will come in."
Ross appeared via Zoom in Miami-Dade bond court Thursday morning, where Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Mindy Glazer said she had reviewed the arrest report and found probable cause in the case.
During the hearing, Horenstein noted that Ross is a celebrity and asked that his client's release be expedited. The judge set Ross' bond at $4,000 on the battery by strangulation charge and $1,000 on the misdemeanor battery charge, for a total of $5,000.
Ross bonded out late Thursday morning.
Glazer also issued a stay-away order involving the alleged victim, identified in court by her initials. Ross was ordered to have no direct or indirect contact with the alleged victim, including through third parties, social media or other electronic means, and to stay away from the person's home, workplace or school.
Ross was also ordered to surrender any firearms and concealed weapons and was prohibited from possessing firearms. The judge also ordered him not to engage in criminal activity or use illegal drugs while the case is pending.
His arraignment is scheduled for Oct. 22.
Ross, a Miami-area native known for songs including "Hustlin'," has been a prominent figure in hip-hop for two decades.
Nikiya  Carrero contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: ‘Carrie’ Has Power but Doesn’t Quite Stick the Landing
articles.title_zh: ‘Carrie’ Has Power but Doesn’t Quite Stick the Landing
articles.content_orig:
There is a very real possibility that were Stephen King to write Carrie today, it would read an awful lot like Mike Flanagan ‘s Carrie , an eight-episode drama series produced for Amazon .
This is the best and worst thing about the new and distinctly non-canonical take, which continues a relationship between Flanagan and King that includes Gerald’s Game , Doctor Sleep and The Life of Chuck (as well as Midnight Mass , which wasn’t based on a Stephen King work, but felt like it ought to have been). The show also extends Flanagan’s record of taking slender texts — The Haunting of Hill House , The Turn of the Screw , The Fall of the House of Usher — and expanding them in unexpected and often impressive ways.
The question is whether or not Carrie is a text that benefits from expansion.
The novel was written before King had the clout (or possibly the desire or drug intake) to unleash 1,000+-page novels into the world and, as a result, it’s marvelously and uncharacteristically small. It’s primarily the story of one young woman coming into astonishing powers that manifest themselves in one horrifying event, free from broader context or richer mythology. Carrie isn’t my favorite King book, but it may be the most immaculately contained example of the master at work.
Another thing about Carrie that cannot be said about most of King’s work is that it was adapted perfectly on the first try. Brian De Palma’s 1976 film has a career-topping performance from Sissy Spacek and multiple set pieces that could fight for a place on the genre’s Mt. Rushmore. Despite that perfection, Hollywood deigned to produce a sequel, a TV movie and a 2013 remake , all well-acted in their central roles and all largely forgotten.
Flanagan is appropriately respectful of De Palma’s film, with nods ranging from outright visual homage to the names of several supporting characters to a fleeting glimpse at a movie theater marquee that made me snort aloud. But unlike the subsequent directors who tackled the material, he has a very clear sense of what he wants to do with it, what he wants to say.
Amazon’s Carrie is probably the adaptation of Carrie that 2026 and the current TV landscape deserve, a collection of big authorial choices that are at best admirable and at worst defensible. But it probably wasn’t the adaptation of Carrie that I wanted. Kudos for its topicality and its performances, especially that of star Summer H. Howell , but this Carrie is finally less distinctive and far less scary than it should be.
Flanagan, director of four of the season’s episodes, starts off with an obligatory in medias res snapshot of news footage and 911 call logs from fires and devastation in the town of Chamberlain, before we go back a year to the death of a construction worker (Tahmoh Penikett’s Ralph White). When authorities go to the White home, they’re surprised to discover Ralph’s stern and religious wife ( Samantha Sloyan ‘s Margaret), as well as a teenage daughter (Howell’s Carrie) who has been home-schooled and, apparently, has never left the house.
In order to retain the house and custody, Margaret has to get a job at a big box store, while Carrie has to go to the local public school.
Carrie is socially maladjusted, but she’s got a good attitude and arrives at school eager to make friends and quote from Anne of Green Gables .
This is not exactly what happens.
Yes, the spineless but amiable principal ( Matthew Lillard ), cool young gym teacher Rita ( Amber Midthunder ) and gay guidance counselor Peter ( Tim Bagley ) want to ease her transition, and class president Sue Snell ( Siena Agudong ) reaches out agreeably. But high school is hard enough if you’re “normal” and Carrie White isn’t normal, in or out of quotation marks.
Carrie’s soon being picked on by Sue’s best friend, Christine ( Alison Thornton ), a spoiled rich girl with family issues and insecurities that she’s happy to redirect at the peculiar new kid who doesn’t even understand how to behave during live shooter drills.
Did I mention that when Carrie gets sad or angry, things tend to shake and, occasionally, rocks fall from the sky onto the White house?
And did I mention that Carrie hasn’t had her first period and that her mother, a big proponent of the “prayer closet” when it comes to domestic discipline, didn’t prepare her in any way for the magic of menstruation?
Oh and one more thing I maybe should mention: Somebody is interviewing the survivors of whatever bad thing happens in the opening scene. Is it the police? A documentary director? And why are the things people are saying about Carrie and the disaster mighty different from what fans of the property might be expecting?
Flanagan understands Carrie , but there are points where he acts like nobody else has ever understood it before, like Carrie is some deeply coded riddle of a novel rather than an effectively blunt allegory about how nothing confounds and terrifies society like a teenage girl.
I fully endorse Flanagan’s attempts to connect Carrie White to a history of ill-fated extraordinary young women, from Joan of Arc on, but might it have been done in a way that didn’t feel cribbed from the “Claimants of telekinetic abilities” section on the Telekinesis Wikipedia page?
I ask this because the third episode begins with an unseen narrator documenting historical case studies with an ordered list that is pretty literally taken from the “Claimants of telekinetic abilities” section on the Telekinesis Wikipedia page.
Flanagan also understands the life of the modern American teen and he knows that if it was hard to grow up different in the 1970s, things have only become more difficult with the pervasive looming specter of school shootings, social media and general societal fragmentation.
So just imagine being a teen today, having your first period in the middle of a changing room, having a well-deserved meltdown, and having every single one of your malevolent classmates capable of filming the moment and distributing it for the world.
It sucks to be a teen, it sucks to be Carrie White, and Mike Flanagan is out there enumerating all of the ways. In fact, given that the added running time lets us spend more time with the teenage characters and their well-meaning (mostly) but thoroughly ineffectual teachers and administrators, what Amazon’s Carrie resembles far more than Carrie is Netflix’s 13 Reasons Why — the good first season not the two subsequent awful seasons. That isn’t the worst thing in the world, but there are stretches when Carrie ceases to be a show about an adolescent girl with budding telekinesis and instead becomes a show about a different adolescent girl with a mean Instagram feed that causes fights.
Freed from the need to tightly focus, Flanagan loosens up, with some benefits.
Margaret White, a one-dimensional and unexplained fundamentalist nightmare on the page and in previous adaptations, becomes a fully explained fundamentalist nightmare here. Sloyan, like co-stars including Rahul Kohli , Michael Trucco and Kate Siegel, is a regular member of the Flanagan troupe and takes advantage of the opportunity to make the character terrifying in a way that will be recognizable to anybody who has watched a televised school board meeting from many parts of the country in recent years. Margaret is prone to verbal abuse and cruelty, but it comes from a place of love — conspiracy theory-fueled, religiously confusing love.
Margaret looks and behaves like people we may currently know, rather than just being a monstrous shut-in raving about her daughter’s “dirty pillows.” That means she’ll probably offend some people, which means Flanagan and Sloyan did something right.
Bagley is hugely sympathetic, Lillard flawed-but-sympathetic and Midthunder extremely likable as a teacher capable of admitting that only a few years earlier, she might have been one of the mean girls bullying Carrie. articles.title_orig: Walmart is using light-up digital shelf labels to help shoppers and employees find items
articles.title_zh: Walmart is using light-up digital shelf labels to help shoppers and employees find items
articles.content_orig:
Walmart is aiming to make it as easy as possible for its customers to find exactly what they want.
The retailer is leveraging three new tools tied to its digital shelf labels for both customers and store associates to better find products. It's the latest part of the company's push to modernize its technology and incorporate artificial intelligence into its business.
"We are people-led, tech-powered," said Greg Cathey, Walmart's senior vice president of digital transformation. "But the way we look at it is AI as a way to help associates do their job and free up time to allow them to invest in what they love to do most, which is spend more time with customers and their fellow associates."
The new feature for shoppers, called Shop to Light, allows customers to find specific products on the Walmart app, navigate to the correct aisle in the store and then flash the digital shelf label of the product to locate it. The retailer is now incorporating it widely following a pilot program.
That tool is also paired with Pick to Light and Stock to Light, which use the same capabilities to help store associates pick items for digital orders and stock products. All three features will be rolled out to stores companywide by the holiday season, Cathey said.
"This is a use case that customers have asked us for, associates have asked us for," Cathey said. "It gives them time back, and I think if you look at a lot of what we're trying to do, it's all around convenience and being able to help associates and customers free up that time to invest it where they want."
The rollout comes as convenience and speed — particularly in the delivery and pickup segments — have become critical pieces of Walmart's efforts to increase sales. While Walmart's business has grown steadily, and its e-commerce sales continue to soar, investor concerns about its comparable sales and revenue outlook weighed on its stock after its most recent earnings report in August.
Walmart stores carry roughly 120,000 items. Cathey said it's a priority for the company to provide that large range of products while making it easier for customers to locate precise items.
While the company does not publicly share any financial aspects of the program, Cathey said the new features at pilot stores allow associates and customers to have more time while shopping and stocking. The Shop to Light feature has already seen 5 million flashes from customers since it began rolling out to limited locations this summer.
He said these new features will be especially important as the retailer heads into the busy holiday season, and the company views them as "a big win" for time savings.
Walmart began using digital shelf labels, as opposed to paper labels, to allow automatic and systemwide price changes to be rolled out at once. The company currently has more than 4,300 stores with digital shelf labels, and expects them to be installed across the chain by the end of the year, according to Walmart.
He added that the label prices are changed overnight, when customers aren't in the store, and the system has human oversight as well to ensure it has "robust governance" and doesn't make mistakes. Currently, roughly 90% of the sections within the store have digital shelf labels, he said.
"We don't look at it as technology for technology's sake," Cathey said. "So we always have a human in the loop, and we're very focused on human judgment and their ability to make decisions."
Walmart has been investing in its technology to modernize the business on both the consumer-facing side and in internal operations.
It's rolled out an AI agent to help customers with shopping, automated its supply chain, invested in radio frequency identification tags and set the stage for agentic commerce as it embraces AI. It's also spent billions on modernizing its store locations.
On Walmart's most recent earnings call, its CEO, John Furner, said the company is seeing significant returns on its technology strategies, including its investments in AI.
"We believe AI will improve nearly every part of our business by making shopping better, and our associates' work easier," he said.
Still, digital shelf labels and the company's AI push have sparked backlash. They have raised concerns about dynamic pricing and fears that digital labels could lead to price surges or privacy issues with collecting shopping data from customers.
But in an open letter last week, Furner said the company is continuing to "price the product, not the person," adding the retailer does not plan to use customer information to set prices.
"Your income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay won't change the price," Furner wrote.
Cathey, who's been in his position for nearly a year, said his biggest priority when taking over the role was to focus on accelerating the speed of the technology that Walmart uses while keeping human oversight.
Several state legislatures, including New Jersey, have passed measures to restrict digital shelf labels over pricing concerns. Walmart said it has the feature in all of its stores in New Jersey.
Walmart in a statement called the policy an "overreaction, as digital shelf labels are not a tool for surveillance pricing and are simply a modern way to display prices."
Walmart has also invested in drone delivery – which has come under similar scrutiny over privacy concerns – to deliver products to customers in as fast as 30 minutes. That delivery option is available in select states, including Texas and Florida.
Ultimately, Cathey said the new digital shelf label features are all part of the company's bigger goal to ensure that store associates have more time to help meet the individual needs of customers.
And while investors debate whether physical retail or e-commerce is more important to the company's business, Cathey said the new features show that both go hand in hand.
"It's not one or the other anymore. It's both," he said. "We don't look at it as a store or an e-commerce fulfillment. They're actually one and the same."

﻿The HP OmniBook 5 14 looks like a Neo wannabe right down to its 8GB of RAM and colors, but it seems a compelling competitor.
HP is announcing a new laptop that’s squarely aimed at Apple’s MacBook Neo . The 2026 HP OmniBook 5 14 starts at $699.99 with an Intel Core 5 315 “Wildcat Lake” processor, 8GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. Much of that sounds pretty familiar, being in lockstep with both Apple’s Neo and its recent competition from Dell , Asus , and Acer — the HP even offers a similar four color options in silver, pink, blue, and green. But one thing that separates the OmniBook is its inclusion of an OLED display on all configs.
The OmniBook 5 14 can be configured much higher, with up to a Core 7 350 chip, 16GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, but all models include a 1080p webcam, dual speakers, HDMI, 3.5mm audio jack, and just two 10Gbps USB-C ports. And while the inclusion of OLED across the range is a major draw to the new OmniBook, the base config only has a passable 1920 x 1200 resolution and 300 nits of max brightness on its non-touch panel. A touchscreen version will be available when the OmniBook 5 launches in October, but a version with a 2560 x 1600 resolution OLED and 400 nits of brightness isn’t coming until March 2027.
While the OmniBook 5 14 doesn’t seem poised to best the MacBook Neo in raw processing power (based on our other reviews of Wildcat Lake laptops ) or screen brightness, it’s quite thin, light, and colorful. HP even gave it the nicer, sleeker lid logo usually reserved for pricier models. It starts at just 2.56 pounds, and it’s as thin as 0.46 inches / 11.7mm. That’s slightly lighter and thinner than a Neo. And I’d expect its Wildcat Lake chips to offer some good-to-great battery life. But we’ll have to see how it delivers in actual testing.
Alongside the OmniBook 5 14, HP is also announcing a new ProBook 4 G2iS business laptop that it claims at 0.47 inches / 12mm is its “thinnest business notebook.” It’ll also start with Intel Wildcat Lake chips, 8GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD when it launches in December, but there’s no price yet.

When the Chicago Cubs began the 2026 season 27-12, a stretch that included two 10-game winning streaks, many of us thought, “Hey — maybe this year can be something special.”
Well. You know what happened after that. A 10-game losing streak. Injuries. Guys not producing. The bullpen imploding multiple times. After 27-12, they were just 62-61 — one game worse than the Marlins over that span. Sheesh.
And then, a Wild Card Series in which the Cubs offense pretty much vanished. That’s the story of Game 2, a 4-1 loss to the Padres that eliminated the Cubs from the 2026 postseason, almost as if they weren’t even there to begin with.
I could end this recap right there, because what more is there to say, really?
Nevertheless, you come here for game recaps and since this was the last Cubs game of 2026, let’s look at what happened.
One pitch into the bottom of the first inning, the Cubs were already ahead of Game 1 because, well, Fernando Tatis Jr. did not hit Kevin Gausman’s first pitch out of the yard. So, progress?
That progress lasted one inning. In the second, Ty France doubled and stopped at third on a single by Jackson Merrill. Xander Bogaerts singled in France, with Merrill stopping at third, where he scored on a sacrifice fly by Ethan Salas. Incidentally, Salas, who won’t turn 21 until next June, became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a MLB postseason game, breaking the record set by Atlanta catcher Bob Didier in 1969.
The 2-0 score is where the game stayed until the top of the fourth, when the Cubs finally broke through onto the board for the first time in this series.
Seiya Suzuki hit a one-out single and Ian Happ walked.
Nico Hoerner’s single up the middle scored Suzuki to make it 2-1 [VIDEO].
So, down by only one run in the fourth inning, with two runners still on base and only one out? Maybe the Cubs offense could get going here?
It was not to be, although after Matt Shaw struck out, Carson Kelly was hit by a pitch to load the bases.
Dansby Swanson flied to center to end the inning.
About that single run, from BCB’s JohnW53:
The Cubs did not score for the first 12.1 innings of this series.
That is the longest they ever have gone without scoring from the start of a post-season series. They were shut out in Game 1 of three previous series.
In the 1918 World Series vs. the Red Sox and 2015 Division Series vs. the Cardinals, they scored with one out in the second inning of Game 2.
In the 2016 World Series, they scored with one out in the first inning of Game 2.
The one-run deficit did not last long. Gausman struck out Merrill to start the fourth, but Bogaerts then doubled. Craig Counsell opted to bring in Daniel Palencia, who struck out Salas.
Then the Padres sent up Gavin Sheets to bat for Austin Hays. Sheets entered this game with career numbers of .297/.348/.484 with three home runs in 69 plate appearances against the Cubs during the regular season. You could have seen this coming all the way from San Diego to Chicago [VIDEO].
Palencia then hit Jake Cronenworth with a pitch, and the San Diego crowd booed as if that had been intentional; clearly, it was not — Palencia was just struggling with command.
The score might have been worse if not for this nice grab by Pete Crow-Armstrong off Tatis to end the inning [VIDEO] .
So at least we got a nice defensive memory from PCA from this series, even as his offense was silent — 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series.
That fourth inning was basically it. Palencia, David Peterson and Ryan Zeferjahn held the Padres scoreless the rest of the way, four combined shutout innings with four strikeouts. Meanwhile, the Cubs had just three more baserunners after the fourth. Michael Busch walked with two out in the fifth. Tyrone Taylor, batting for Busch, singled with one out in the eighth but was erased when Suzuki hit into a double play. Nico Hoerner doubled with one out in the ninth but was stranded. The Cubs went 1-for-8 with RISP in this game. If they’d hit in those situations would the result have been any different? I’m thinking probably not.
These two games in San Diego were a hallmark of this team, just as the offensive outbursts that had the 2026 Cubs lead MLB in runs also were. It was a real feast-or-famine season — long stretches where the offense could do no wrong, and others where the hitters just did not show up at all.
Here’s PCA on the season-ending loss [VIDEO].
Here are some postgame remarks from Alex Bregman [VIDEO].
Bregman, whose previous postseason performance was one of the reasons the Cubs signed him, went 0-for-8 in this series with four strikeouts.
Lastly, here are Craig Counsell’s postgame remarks [VIDEO].
Would the result of this series have been any different if the Cubs had won two more regular-season games and had home field? Probably not; it’s clear by watching these two games that the Padres were on a roll, which began over the last three weeks of the regular season and carried over into this series. Further, it’s very likely that weather would have been a major factor. It rained all day and evening in Chicago Wednesday and it’s still raining here early Thursday morning, which could have thrown scheduling for this series into chaos. In the end, this Cubs team just wasn’t good enough to move on, and you know the reasons, mostly pitching — injuries and ineffectiveness from both starters and relievers. The offense was great — until it wasn’t.
More on the offense from John:
In the two games of this series, the Cubs were 8 for 62, a batting average of .129. That is lower than in any of their 22 previous post-season series since 1901.
They batted .140 in the one-game Wild Card loss in 2018 and .145 in their two-game WC loss in 2020.
Other seasons below .200: .168 in 2017 (10 games) .181 in 1998 (3 games) .194 in 2007 (3 games) .196 in 1906 (6 games)
They batted .233 in 17 games when they won the World Series in 2016.
These are things that Cubs President of Baseball Operations Jed Hoyer will have to address this offseason, and that brings me to the upcoming uncertainty. Normally when a Cubs season ends, I’d tell you the next date we will see a Chicago Cubs team on the field the following year. They are scheduled to take the field Friday, Feb. 19, 2027 against the A’s at Ho Ho Kam Stadium in Mesa, Arizona. But with a looming owners’ lockout likely happening when the current MLB/MLBPA collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, there’s no guarantee that the 2027 Spring Training schedule — or regular season schedule — will be played as currently listed.
And so we wait. For developments, as is often said here.
In the meantime, stick around. We’ll have game threads here for all the remaining postseason games, including tonight’s decisive Phillies/Braves Game 3, which will begin at 7 p.m. CT (game thread will post at 6 p.m. CT). And of course, we’ll cover all the MLB offseason labor news and other baseball news here.
As is my custom, I will wrap my last game recap of the year by quoting from the late Commissioner Bart Giamatti’s “The Green Fields of the Mind” — quite appropriate today with the Chicago area weather.
It breaks your heart. It is designed to break your heart. The game begins in the spring, when everything else begins again, and it blossoms in the summer, filling the afternoons and evenings, and then as soon as the chill rains come, it stops and leaves you to face the fall alone. You count on it, rely on it to buffer the passage of time, to keep the memory of sunshine and high skies alive, and then just when the days are all twilight, when you need it most, it stops.

Facing new competition in the audiobook market from Spotify, Audible is turning to AI and other technology to enhance the listening experience. On Thursday, the Amazon-owned company introduced three new features that will allow listeners to explore a book’s characters, engage in interactive stories, and view additional imagery and bonus information about landmarks or places mentioned in the book.
If you’re thinking the last would be great for highlighting the different courts’ locations in Sarah J. Maas’ faerie realm of Prythian, I must disappoint you. The feature will first arrive in just one title for now, “The Cultural Tutor: A Modern Guide to History, Art and Philosophy in 49 Short Chapters” by Sheehan Quirke, which focuses on making culture more accessible by teaching about poetry, art, architecture, geography, and more in short lessons.
The other new features, a character guide and interactive stories, are also starting off fairly small.
With Audible’s October 1 release of its Audible Original “Dracula,” the character guide will help listeners keep track of the cast of characters in the book, something that’s harder to do when listening than when reading. (The Audible Originals label doesn’t necessarily signal that the content is original, as “Dracula” is not. It means Audible’s own studios have produced the audiobook, memoir, exclusive series, podcast, or performance.)
In “Dracula,” the character guide will display who’s speaking in real time directly on the player page so listeners don’t get lost. It will also provide spoiler-free character cards, which showcase the narrator behind the voice and their bio. Audible says users will later be able to interact with the guide to ask questions about the story as it unfolds.
Other audiobooks gaining access to the character guide include the Audible Original of George Orwell’s “1984” and the forthcoming Audible Original “Exoplanet” from writer Benjamin Percy and executive producer Andy Weir (author of “Project Hail Mary” and “The Martian”).
A third feature, interactive stories, will also come to “Dracula” and “Exoplanet.”
Here, the idea is to bring the listener into the story through a bonus experience in which they interact with a book’s character. Powered by generative AI, the feature lets listeners interact with Dracula’s servant, Renfield, in the new Audible Original.
The character will speak first, giving the listener a role, goal, and stakes, and the listener then responds in their own words. The character will react to what’s said in real time.
Audible says the creators are involved in the foundations of the interactive stories, so the stories stay grounded in what’s happening in the book. Or, in the case of something like “Dracula,” the stories are meant to stay faithful to the original creator’s vision.
The changes come as audiobook listenership and revenue grow , with U.S. sales reaching $2.43 billion in 2025. The increased demand can be chalked up to several factors, from the proliferation of the smartphone to people’s increasingly busy schedules that make sitting down to read a book feel like a luxury. One could probably also credit TikTok’s “BookTok” community for pushing reading more into the mainstream — something that’s reflected in the most popular audiobook genres , which overlap with BookTok’s interests in fiction, sci-fi, thrillers, and, of course, romantasy.
“These new features invite listeners into a story in ways that simply weren’t possible before, marking the latest step in our nearly 30-year journey to push audio storytelling forward,” said Audible’s Chief Content Officer Rachel Ghiazza in a statement about the launch. “We’re excited to build on these while working hand in hand with creators, because we know that more time spent with stories benefits everyone who helps bring them to life.”
The company says the features are currently in a beta test, and the plan is to expand to more titles over time.

Kindles don’t usually change much with each new version, but Amazon is launching next-generation models today that look and feel a whole lot nicer. The base Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft are a millimeter thinner and 30 percent faster at opening books, and their power buttons have moved from the bottom to the right edge near the top.
They ship in vibrant new colors with a soft-touch plastic case, and, for the first time, there’s the option for a couple shades of aluminum, giving them a higher-end look and feel, not to mention double the storage of the plastic version (32GB versus 16GB). Amazon VP of Kindle Kevin Keith told The Verge that they all feature user-replaceable batteries to be in compliance with EU regulations , too.
The updated base Kindle is available today starting at $149.99 in a new purple color called ube and a plainer graphite color. It comes with 16GB of storage and lockscreen ads, and it looks nicer than the last-gen version, thanks to a seamless transition from frame to screen, moving on from the old design that had a recessed display.
New for this revision is the choice of aluminum , which bumps the price up to $189.99, doubles the storage, and ditches ads. The Kindle in aluminum is a very nice, compact thing to hold, especially in its new folio case that it can magnetically attach to. Though, at $239.98 all together ($189.99 for the e-reader and $49.99 for the case), you’re firmly in the territory of the Paperwhite, with its more pixel-dense and auto-dimming screen for $199.99 .
The display specs for the new Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (coming October 28th, available to preorder now) haven’t changed, though the color options have. The new plastic and aluminum colors available for each cover the entirety of the e-readers, not just their backsides. Amazon’s Keith credits a new technique of applying a black layer between the edges of the panel to prevent the case’s color from visually bleeding onto the screen.
The aluminum options for the Paperwhite and Colorsoft, costing $249.99 and $319.99 , respectively, include more than the base Kindle’s high-end version. These are the new Signature Edition versions, with pogo pins on their rear that are compatible with a $79.99 page-turn magnetic case that adds physical page-turning buttons a la the Kindle Oasis. Wireless charging isn’t offered in the new Signature Editions. Amazon will sell a $59.99 charging dock that can charge this edition upright and attaches via pogo pins.
Amazon is also adding a remote to the lineup, the Kindle Click. Amazon’s $34.99 Bluetooth remote lets you turn pages when you’re away from your device, with side-mounted buttons to adjust screen brightness. The remote’s main buttons are soft and quiet to press, and it’s lightweight, with a wrist strap to keep it from easily disappearing. It can recharge via USB-C, and it’s compatible with Kindles from 2024 or later.
Though we still seem be in the midst of Apple’s hardware launch season , Amazon has dropped a few new products so far in the past week, including a new Fire TV Stick 4K that can be powered directly through your TV’s USB port instead of requiring a power brick.
Correction, October 1st, 9:32am ET : The Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft launch October 28th, not today, as the article originally stated.

The horrors of modern high school loom large in Mike Flanagan’s “Carrie,” a series adaptation of Stephen King’s 52-year-old novel that’s keen to speak to today’s youth.
When Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) first enters Ewen P.H.S. after a lifetime of homeschooling, she’s greeted with metal detectors at the front doors, zombified students staring at their phones, and intrusive parents eager to contort curriculums on behalf of their kids. (Surprisingly, entitled adults aren’t even the most intrusive example of a damaged American psyche). On top of all that , she still has to handle classic teenage hardships like a tyrannical mother (although with this hormonal 16-year-old, any claims of having a certified wackjob for a mom would be accurate), nerd-induced ostracism (she loves to quote books that nobody but her teachers have read), and bullying — live in-person and via social media.
Entering a new school can feel like a lot to anyone, whether they’re raised in a traditional education system surrounded by friends, or learning math from Bible verses while isolated with doomsday-prepper parents. But Carrie stands out. She is, as a social worker says, “stunningly uninformed” — living her entire life without access to the internet, libraries, phones, or a community of disparate voices. Yet she’s also defiantly openhearted, even after her father dies at the start of our story. When the police arrive to break the news — finding Carrie and Margaret (Samantha Sloyan) hiding in a “prayer closet” — her mother’s irate fear is all but erased by Carrie’s elated smile. She’s not like her mom, and she’s not like the rest of us. She’s closer to an alien discovering Earth, as eager to explore as she is to turn strangers into friends.
But she’s also not like the rest of us — and kind of like some people’s idea of aliens — in that she can crush a car with her mind.
Within the genre staples and character beats familiar to fans of King’s novel (and Brian De Palma’s Oscar-nominated 1976 film), the 2026 version of “Carrie” loses its way. Carrie’s telekinesis leaks out in drips and drabs, as if Flanagan is as embarrassed by his lead character’s abnormality as a teenager trying to hide an acne flare-up. She rarely talks about her burgeoning ability, and aside from the inevitable, overdrawn, and underwhelming meltdown at prom, her superpower struggles to manifest into resonant frights.
But the horror is also hemmed in by one of the new “Carrie’s” core strengths: sympathy. Despite an opening montage in which a slew of witnesses debate whether Carrie is a victim or a bully, a hero or a monster, the series only sees her one way. It’s too timid to embrace evil, even as a temptation, and that limits its capacity to explore the human condition beyond mourning our collective lack of compassion.
As if there was any doubt, Flanagan’s adaptation extends an understanding embrace not just to Carrie, but her classmates, too. There’s Sue Snell (Siena Agudong), a friendly popular girl who’s dating “the hottest guy in school,” Tommy Ross (Joel Oulette), when she’s not hanging out with her best friend, Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton). While Tommy is Sue’s soulmate in kindness (quiet, sensitive, and unafraid to speak up for the unjustly maligned, he’s almost too good to be believed), Chris is a self-described “bitch” who promises to “never apologize for it.”
She never does, but she also doesn’t have to. “Carrie” does the apologizing for her, saddling Chris with a douchebag dad (Michael Trucco) so one-note he feels teleported in from a different show. While all the other characters show glimmers of decency, Mr. Hargensen’s disdain for his own daughter provides all the motivation Chris needs to vent her frustrations on the weird new girl, while every so often regretting how far her misplaced fury takes her. A locker room incident breeds resentment and mockery, before ballooning into further disputes that should prove familiar to anyone who attended a sizable school.
Chris is an instigator, but “Carrie’s” only real villains are adults. The series posits American society is letting down our kids and more specifically calls out parents for repressing, manipulating, and otherwise contaminating their natural nobilities. Unfortunately, the main representative of those messages is a mess.
Margaret White is a misanthrope and a hypocrite. She speaks down to everyone as if they only comprehend single-syllable words and rails against teachers for pushing an agenda in the same breath she uses to demand they enforce her will across the entire school. Her flaws are obvious, which makes her easy to root against, but her virtues, as few as they may be, don’t distinguish Margaret from Chris’ soulless father. She’s more controlling, sure, but she’s just as monotonous and predictable, which makes Carrie’s growing distrust in her own mother a tension-free wait for a foregone conclusion. With a little more development, Margaret could’ve been a complex, charismatic, and challenging force. Instead, she’s just a representative.
While “Carrie” lands closer to “The Midnight Club” than “Midnight Mass” in its showrunner’s oeuvre, it makes the most of Flanagan’s mesmeric monologues (even if some prove redundant), moves through its story smoothly (when it’s not planting seeds to extend beyond the book, the details of which I’m embargoed from bringing up), and features a slew of solid performances.
Some clunky plot maneuverings spare Howell the tricky heel turn you’d expect for the finale’s extended prom-tastrophe, but they allow the actor to settle into her affecting innocence. This version of Carrie could easily prove grating in the same way she does to her cynical tormentors — too oblivious, too sincere, too nice — but she’s always endearing, thanks in large part to Howell’s nuanced commitment to drawing out her awakening. Thornton is equally effective on the other end of the spectrum. As Chris succumbs to her worst instincts, you can appreciate her hesitancy as well as her relish, sometimes at the same time.
In scenes big and small, Flanagan’s trademark empathy is moving and earned, creating timely interpretations of age-old conflicts and eloquent emotional beats between characters in conflict. But it’s also flattening, for Carrie and for “Carrie.” The first season (of an intended three ) is attuned to its allegory about the horrors of high school, but it would never be confused with a horror show — not without its franchise baggage — and the imbalance makes for a teen drama that’s blunt, preachy, and broad.
Despite earnestly engaging with its younger characters while throwing the olds to the wolves, the series ultimately feels like it’s told from a parent’s perspective. It’s a plea instead of a roar, and the modern world, with all its problems, calls for screams.
“Carrie” premieres Wednesday, October 7 on Amazon Prime Video . All eight episodes of the first season will be released at once.

articles.title_zh: Netanyahu says it's too early to determine motive in FlyDubai cockpit stabbing incident
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu indicated to CBS News Wednesday that the motive of the co-pilot accused of stabbing his fellow pilot on a passenger jet bound from Dubai to Tel Aviv was still unknown.
"I don't think it was a hijacking," Netanyahu told "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil.
"I think it looks like a suicide attempt simply because of what this hero Yaniv described when he went in," Netanyahu speculated, referring to Yaniv Hayoun, one of the passengers on the FlyDubai flight who has been credited with entering the cockpit and helping to subdue the attacker.
"This guy was trying to jam the equipment between the two flight seats, the pilot seats," Netanyahu said of the co-pilot, whose identity has not been revealed. "He wasn't sitting in the pilot seat trying to stabilize the plane, he was trying to jam the equipment."
Speaking Thursday to Fox News, Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning. In He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
According to Israeli officials, on Wednesday morning local time, the FlyDubai jet was about two hours into its flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when the co-pilot stabbed the captain.
Per data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News, the plane then plunged about 17,000 feet, climbed 5,000 feet, and then fell another 7,000 feet before stabilizing.
Israeli officials and passengers said the captain, an Indian national, was able to fight off his co-pilot and unlock the cockpit door. Witnesses recounted how a group of passengers and crew members then stormed the cockpit and subdued the co-pilot.
Two off-duty pilots then took control of the plane and made an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. There were 174 people on board, Israeli officials said. Most of the passengers later boarded a replacement FlyDubai plane and were flown to Ben Gurion International Airport, arriving Wednesday night.
An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker, whose name has not been released, was born in Oman and holds Omani citizenship, but the Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
Netanyahu told CBS News he was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia.
"He'll be, I assume, moved very quickly to Dubai," Netanyahu told CBS News, adding that Israeli authorities will "join the interrogation and find out what happened there exactly."
A senior Israeli official told CBS News' Dov Lieber on Thursday that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan personally told Netanyahu on Wednesday that he expected Saudi authorities to transfer the pilot to the UAE for questioning.
Asked if he thought the incident could have stemmed from a mental health issue and not an act of terrorism, Netanyahu said, "it could be, I don't know, we'll find out soon."
"We've had signs that Iran, and particularly through its proxies, was intending to heighten terrorist attacks against Israel and Israeli nationals abroad," Netanyahu added. "But I think it's too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here. I think we'll find out, won't take a long time."
No definitive motive for the stabbing has been determined by authorities. An Israeli security official previously told CBS News that investigators were looking into the possibility that the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack.
"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," FlyDubai said in its own statement. It urged "all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts."

articles.title_zh: Microsoft Has A Mountain To Climb To Address Windows 11 Optimizations, But Newest 26H2 Update Tackles Memory Usage; 8GB RAM Systems Left Out
articles.content_orig:
The newest Windows 11 version 26H2 update has begun rolling out to millions of users worldwide, with some of them commenting that the latest iteration has introduced some optimizations regarding memory usage. Unfortunately, if you only have 8GB of RAM installed, then you’re probably excluded.
It appears that Microsoft hasn’t quite stuck with its promises of making Windows 11 more memory efficient for systems equipped with 8GB of memory . On Reddit , user “shutter_singh” has shown that RAM usage has decreased by 2GB after installing the latest update, but here’s the catch. If you look at the post below, his system is equipped with 48GB RAM, so it’s highly unlikely that a 2GB reduction will make or break his Windows 11 experience.
On the flipside, another Redditor with the handle “HenryDaGodzilla,” says that there was no change in the RAM usage after updating to version 26H2, and that’s probably because he’s using a Windows 11 system equipped with 8GB RAM instead of 48GB, with the former consuming a whopping 96 percent (7.4GB) of total system memory. On X, @SoyITPro notes that with the same update, his RAM consumption reduced from 9.1GB to 7.5GB.
However, he shares his Task Manager screenshot, revealing that he’s running 32GB of RAM, making it two instances where the Windows 11 26H2 update is benefiting systems with a higher memory count. A new market intelligence report says that the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are selling well in China , making Apple the best-selling brand in the country during the launch week.
Counterpoint Research has said there are three reasons for the popularity of Apple’s latest iPhone …
Rising costs have seen overall sales of new smartphones in China decline 17% year on year since July, according to Counterpoint Research’s China Weekly Smartphone Sell-Out Tracker. However, the firm reports that this trend was reversed by the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro.
During the first three days of its sales (which accounted for only three days in Week 38), the iPhone 18 Pro series recorded 12% YoY growth compared with the iPhone sales. The strong initial performance helped Apple move into the No. 1 spot in sales in Week 38, with a 33% share of China’s smartphone market.
Counterpoint suggests there are three reasons underlying the popularity of the new model.
First, the delayed launch of the base iPhone 18. Because Apple has launched the two iPhone 18 Pro models well ahead of the standard model, some may have decided to upgrade to the premium version rather than wait.
Second, rising prices across all premium smartphones have led to consumers being willing to pay higher prices than would previously have been the case. Apple has absorbed some of the increased component costs, making the iPhone 18 Pro comparatively better value.
Third is what Counterpoint describes as “aggressive channel support,” generally meaning heavy advertising and promotions by retailers and carriers.

articles.title_orig: Ex-frat leader at Arizona university gets jail time after pledge died of alcohol poisoning
articles.title_zh: Ex-frat leader at Arizona university gets jail time after pledge died of alcohol poisoning
articles.content_orig:
Flagstaff — A former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader was sentenced to two months in jail Wednesday for his role in a hazing that led to the death of a pledge.
Carter Eslick, 20, also received three years of supervised probation during a sentencing hearing in Coconino County Superior Court. Eslick had pleaded guilty to a felony hazing charge in the Jan. 31 death of Colin Daniel Martinez, 18, at an off-campus house.
An autopsy found Martinez died of alcohol poisoning with a blood-alcohol content of 0.425% — more than five times the state's legal limit for drivers 21 and over.
Martinez was among four Delta Tau Delta pledges who shared two bottles of vodka to ensure they vomited, according to court documents. Witnesses reported adjusting Martinez's sleeping position and checking his pulse and breathing to look for signs of alcohol poisoning throughout the night, the documents said.
Martinez's parents appeared remotely in court, still grieving their son, and said they want accountability and reform within Greek life, CBS Phoenix affiliate KPHO-TV reported .
Eslick was the fraternity's pledge master at the time and was responsible for welcoming new members.
The hearing began with testimony from five of Eslick's friends and family members who attested to his character while warning about the dangers of fraternity culture, KPHO noted.
"While trying to teach my children these things, I realized I failed to teach him or explain to them, and in those gaps, toxic influence and toxic communities have stepped in," said Cody Eslick, Carter's father.
Carter Eslick apologized to Martinez's family, KPHO said.
"I am so incredibly deeply sorry for the events that happened on Jan. 31, and I take full responsibility for the hand I played in that ritual," Eslick said. "And if I had known that one day somebody's life could be in my hands, there is no way in hell I would have ever looked that way."
Coconino County Attorney Ammon Barker said no sentence can undo the harm to the Martinez family.
"My hope is that this case helps people understand the serious dangers of hazing and encourages them to speak up and intervene before another family experiences this kind of loss," Barker said in a statement.
Judge Stacy Krueger said Eslick knew what he did was dangerous and was troubled that no one spoke out against it.
Eslick could face additional jail time if he doesn't meet the conditions of probation, which include creating and delivering 305 anti-hazing presentations and keeping the court updated on his progress. He also can't use alcohol or drugs unless prescribed.
The university suspended the fraternity after Martinez's death, and the national organization later closed the NAU chapter.

A medical helicopter crashed off Catalina Island near Los Angeles , killing two people and leaving two hospitalized, authorities said.
Rescuers early on Thursday searched for a fifth person who was reported to be in the aircraft and was missing, the Los Angeles county fire department said in a social media post.
First responders were called to the crash shortly before 8pm on Wednesday and pulled four people from the water. Two were pronounced dead at the scene and two were brought in stable condition to hospitals on the mainland, the fire department said.

County firefighters and lifeguards responded to the scene, along with the US Coast Guard and the sheriff’s department, officials said.

articles.title_orig: Britain and France Give Up Landmark Migrant Agreement
articles.title_zh: Britain and France Give Up Landmark Migrant Agreement
articles.content_orig:
Agreement expected to end on Thursday after running for 423 days, during which it has been beset by problems
UK politics live – latest updates
The UK government’s “one in, one out” deal with France , which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said.
The deal involved returning to France one asylum seeker who had arrived in the UK in a small boat, in exchange for another brought legally to the UK from France. It lasted 423 days – from 10 July 2025 until 1 October 2026.
The UK’s official explanation was that it had not been able to scale up the numbers of asylum seekers involved as much as it would have liked to. However, the scheme was beset with problems. Scores returned to the UK during the scheme because they felt unsafe in France. Some were returned to France a second time while others were allowed to remain in the UK to have their claims processed here. Many were believed to have vanished after being returned to France. Asylum seekers said they were threatened by smugglers because they owed them money and feared being sent back to their home countries or to another European country they had passed through on their journey.
Approximately 1,500 asylum seekers were returned to France, with a similar number brought legally from France to the UK. The numbers removed under the scheme were fewer than the total who arrived in small boats over seven days in the second half of last month. More than 40,000 have arrived in Britain in small boats during the period the deal has been in place.
It is understood France wanted to end the deal because it did not want to carry the weight of accepting small boat arrivals back from the UK alone and instead wanted the rest of Europe to also get involved. Other European countries have so far not agreed to join the scheme. “Why do we have to manage this border on our own?” the French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said at a parliamentary hearing this year. “We believe that France should not have to bear the burden alone, and that it would be better to incorporate it into an agreement between the European Union and the United Kingdom.”
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said at a recent session of the Commons home affairs committee that it was difficult to pinpoint exactly why there had been a reduction of more than 40% in the number of people crossing the Channel so far this year compared with the same period last year. Others say that lower levels of irregular migration into the UK from France in the first five months of this year compared with the same period last year are likely at least partially to be due to a drop in arrivals of irregular migrants to Europe overall. The Home Office said it would continue to remove as many small boat arrivals as possible. But it is not possible to forcibly remove people to unsafe countries such as Iran, Eritrea, Sudan and others, where many on small boats come from.
NGOs such as Medical Justice have condemned the trauma they have documented due to the detention of this group, many of whom are survivors of trafficking or torture. Force was used against one in 10 of 224 asylum seekers during their removal to France in the first three months of this year, according to Home Office freedom of information data. Both the NGO Médecins Sans Frontières and the French health organisation Samusocial , which provides treatment for returnees to France, documented physical and psychological injuries. At the home affairs committee the home secretary suggested these injuries may have been self-inflicted. The Labour MP and committee member Bell Ribeiro-Addy accused the home secretary of “victim blaming” and said there was independent evidence of injuries sustained as a result of use of force.
Successive prime ministers and home secretaries have vowed to stop small boats crossing the Channel. So far none have succeeded. For as long as people flee war and conflict a percentage of them are likely to turn up in the UK by one means or another. The use of return hubs in third countries is under discussion by some European countries although no details have been confirmed.
In a word, overjoyed. “Thank God. You gave me the best news,” said one asylum seeker forcibly returned to France, after hearing the news. He is now considering returning to the UK. Another who is also hoping to return said: “That’s good news. We just hope the UK doesn’t make a worse agreement with a new country.”

articles.title_orig: What we’re reading: China Miéville, Sebastian Barry, Derek Owusu and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in September
articles.title_zh: What we’re reading: China Miéville, Sebastian Barry, Derek Owusu and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in September
articles.content_orig:
Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
I was sideswiped by Giada Scodellaro’s Ruins, Child . A brilliant, strange book that challenged me in the most exhilarating way, with its fractured language and dream-cinema visions, the sense it bestowed of walking through a corridor full of echoes. Echoes of a less elliptical but no-less political kind haunt Jordy Rosenberg’s astounding Night Night Fawn . I guess you could call it a family novel? But it’s at least as much about fascism as it is about the family – as well as about unsettling linkages between the two. And for horrors and rage in a nonfiction register, Jonas Marvin’s The Breaking of the English Working Class is an indispensable – and beautifully written – essay on decades of structural, economic and psychic violence. The feeling it provoked in me brought to mind John Berger’s phrase “undefeated despair”.
The Rouse by China Miéville is published by Picador (£35). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.
I was totally immersed in Whale Fall by Elizabeth O’Connor, a beautifully written story describing a short time in the life of a young woman and her fishing community on an island off the coast of Wales in the 1930s. The simplicity of this tale is underpinned with intriguing moral issues when two anthropologists visit the island to study the lives and history of the islanders. The book is the most poetic I’ve read in a while.
I’ve enjoyed so many books recently. Two I now claim as favourites of all time. The first is Beloved by Toni Morrison . Incredibly late to the party because I was resistant to reading her again having had such a hard time with Sula. But Beloved, in my opinion, is the perfect novel. The second is Pedro Páramo by Juan Rulfo, one of the founding texts of the Latin American tradition of magical realism. It was hard work but so enjoyable, a reminder that challenging can be fun and that it’s possible to tell a story in a variety of ways. Last, I want to mention The Bridge of San Luis Rey by Thornton Wilder. I’ve only just finished it, so coherent feelings are still working themselves out, but in the mix I know there is admiration, pleasure, something life affirming and something ineffable sparked by the religious elements of the novel. I’m almost certain it’s going to join the others as one of my favourites. I’m having a great run.
The Recovery House by Derek Owusu is published by Merky Books (£16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.
In the day, Mario Vargas Llosa by Gerald Martin, a giant ship of a book which, at nearly a thousand pages, will probably steer me through the remains of 2026. In the night, when I cannot sleep, I do as I always do around the date of my birthday: a re-read of all of Jean Rhys. With her, I am on the moonlit deck of the ship and we watch the darkness of a deep sea rush by. For sanity, The Practice of Not Thinking by Ryunosuke Koike: the antidote to botched CBT therapy. For inspiration, For Now by Eileen Myles, concerning the loss of part of their archive and the struggle to hold on to a rent controlled apartment of 40 years. And My Life on the Road by Gloria Steinem. Of course.
after newsletter promotion
If anyone is in a mood to have their psyches calmed and their reading synapses restored, then The Last Chronicle of Barset by Anthony Trollope is the cat’s pyjamas. I was nodding my head recently when Marlon James was saying somewhere that he rated Trollope above Dickens. Not that D is any slouch. I am rereading a book I read for work, and now again just because it’s so excellently done, Army Life in a Black Regiment , by Thomas Wentworth Higginson. Emerson said it was a masterpiece by a writer not known for writing masterpieces(!) The Penguin Classics reissue in the late 1990s also has his correspondence with Emily Dickinson and an account of his one meeting with her, revelatory on many levels. She spoke as she wrote. I was also very admiring of a little book of poems by Kayleigh Jayshree called Mango and Starblush , which Miss Dickinson might have called true poems.

articles.title_orig: Cornell case spotlights 'confusing' web of systems for reporting campus assaults
articles.title_zh: Cornell case spotlights 'confusing' web of systems for reporting campus assaults
articles.content_orig:
"I'm very shocked" - College students react to Cornell University rape investigation
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of sexual assault.
When Mary was a first-year college student, she woke up after a fraternity party with bruises and bite marks all over her body. She says it took her a few days to piece together that she had been sexually assaulted while "blacked out", and to find the strength - and the right avenue - to report the assault.
The man she accused was eventually expelled, but police declined to bring charges because they said there was a lack of physical evidence.
Mary - whose name has been changed to protect her identity - says the process of finding some measure of justice was oftentimes confusing and disappointing.
"Even though it was a positive outcome, it was still so emotionally exhausting and draining, because I had to do all of this in tandem with getting used to being a college student for the first time," said Mary. "In many ways, I had to be my own advocate, gathering all my evidence."
The experience with local police, she added, "left me with a deep sense of disappointment in the system".
How both universities and the criminal justice system respond to these types of assaults on college campuses is once again under the spotlight, after a former student at Cornell University filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was raped by several members of a fraternity two years ago, with prosecutors declining at the time to pursue a case.
What we know about Cornell rape investigation
Mary did not attend Cornell, and her case is not connected with the university. But advocates for survivors of sexual assault say her case, and the Cornell allegations, are emblematic of the larger challenges in responding to sexual assault claims on college campuses specifically.
The confusing web of systems and policies - which varies greatly by college - is one of several reasons why the vast majority of sexual assaults on college campuses, research suggests, go unreported.
"These processes are hard to navigate if you aren't in trauma," said Nancy Chi Cantalupo, an associate professor of law at Wayne State University who has represented victims on college campuses. "If you are in trauma, they're virtually impossible to navigate."
Earlier this month, the former Cornell student known only as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against the Ivy League university, alleging she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. Jane Doe said she had reported the alleged assault to campus police, who interviewed her, and provided information to the district attorney's office. The prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time, but this week, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten re-opened the case.
Both Cornell and Van Houten have defended their handling of the 2024 case. I n a statement , external , the university said it had "conducted an extensive investigation and adjudication over several months and imposed different sanctions based on the findings and circumstances involving each student" in addition to creating a new framework for addressing sexual assault on campus.
Cornell has said it followed the procedures outlined in a federal civil rights law called Title IX. The law mandates that universities follow certain rules about investigating sexual assaults. Cornell said its investigation resulted in the fraternity involved being barred from campus, and that students involved were suspended or expelled.
Typically, after a student reports an assault on campus, the university's Title IX office determines whether the alleged behaviour could constitute a violation of policy.
Eventually, both parties attend a hearing with a panel of faculty members or other mediators to present evidence and testimony in the case before a decision by the school is reached.
One of the biggest challenges sexual assault survivors face is simultaneously navigating the university and the criminal justice system, which "serve different purposes, operate under different rules and timelines, and lead to different outcomes", said Zoey Scheinblum-Brewer, a policy coordinator at the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network, a nonprofit anti-sexual assault organisation.
"Unclear guidance about the options available through these parallel processes can create so much confusion and uncertainty that some students ultimately decide not to report," she said.
Mary said this process at her college was not clear to her when she made the decision to report the assault.
"For me, it would've been nice to know what I was getting into before it all happened. It felt like they were learning the process alongside me," she said of university officials.
While some colleges, like Cornell, have information sharing agreements with local police, Mary was told she had to go to police separately to file a report - a process she found physically exhausting.
Mary's lawyer says there was surveillance footage from the night showing her alleged rapist carrying her "slumped" over, and she had pictures of her bruises and bite marks. But police told Mary they did not have probable cause for an arrest, and that the district attorney wanted to leave it to university administration.
"I was left with this taste that because they knew that the college was 'handling' my investigation, that they could wipe their hands clean of it," she said.
The local police department told the BBC it did not have the details of this particular case. The local district attorney's office did not respond to a request for comment.
University investigations are done behind closed doors, said Helene Weiss, a lawyer who has represented several victims of sexual assault on college campuses. She believes that part of the reason for the secrecy is to protect institutions' reputations.
"The secrecy of the process, it prevents other students from knowing about it. It prevents witnesses from coming forward," she said.
Michael Diamondstein, a Pennsylvania attorney who has represented those accused of sexual misconduct on college campuses, said the secrecy helps protect both the victim and the accused.
"I think when you compare it to what they would face in a courtroom, it's much easier for students and much safer for students. Their name isn't put out there. The news media doesn't get them," he said.
Cornell students have criticised the university's handling of the woman's claims. The Cornell Daily Sun, a student newspaper, published the names of the accused under the headline: "Cornell won't, we will."
In a statement, the college said that federal privacy law "prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individualâ¯students" so it cannot "make a public statement on any other disciplinary response".
Many advocates say there is merit to universities investigating sexual assault complaints separately from the criminal justice system. Prosecuting sexual assault cases is notoriously difficult - a recent systematic review found that less than 10% of sexual assault cases yielded convictions. In a criminal trial, a prosecutor must convince a jury "beyond reasonable doubt" that the accused is guilty. But in a campus tribunal, the burden of proof is lower.
Under Title IX, the university is also required to offer solutions that local law enforcement cannot, like ensuring a student is not in the same class as their alleged abuser while the investigation is ongoing and offering homework extensions, said Scheinblum-Brewer.
This is one of several reasons why victims and advocates for survivors say there are benefits to having two separate avenues, through the university and the criminal justice system.
For Mary, after her case was dropped by the police, pursuing her assault claim through Title IX became the only way for her alleged rapist to face repercussions: an expulsion from college.

articles.title_orig: PS5 emulation is suddenly making big strides on PC
articles.title_zh: PS5 emulation is suddenly making big strides on PC
articles.content_orig:
For a long time, PC gamers could access many PlayStation 5 games only if the publisher invested in a bespoke port (something Sony has recently said it will be scaling back ). Now, though, rapid advancements in PS5 emulators and other tools are making recent PlayStation titles increasingly playable on generic PCs.
SharpEmu was the first of these emulators, advancing from a “very early alpha stage” in May to a current state that can “load the eboot.bin of real games, execute native CPU instructions, and partially handle GPU-related functionality.” The most recent release boasts 10 tested games that reach a “playable” state , including six that developer CursedIfElse says are “fully playable at 60 fps.” That includes simple 2D games like Tetris Forever but also 3D titles like Astro Bot and the PS5 Demon’s Souls remaster running at playable frame rates.
“SharpEmu has prioritized hardware accuracy from the very beginning, and we’re finally starting to see that investment pay off,” CursedIfElse wrote on social media this week . “It was built completely from scratch, and this is how far we’ve come.”
Amid that SharpEmu progress, fellow PS5 emulator KytyPS5 launched its first public version last week . The major expansion of PS4-focused emulator Kyty “can boot 2D games and a selection of 3D games, including titles built with Unreal Engine 4/5, Unity, and custom engines,” according to its GitHub page .
An extensive compatibility list for KytyPS5 already shows 134 titles with “controllable gameplay” on the new emulator, though many of those still include reports of persistent, game-breaking bugs. But you can already find YouTube footage of PS5 titles like Astro’s Playroom and Demon’s Souls running quite capably under the emulator.
On top of those more traditional emulators, AnyPS5 might be the most interesting effort to get PS5 games running on PC. The self-described “tool for automatic executables porting” works kind of like Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit , relinking a PS5 game’s original x86 game code directly to native executable instructions that can run on PC. That puts the effort somewhere between direct static decompilation of a game’s source code and more complete emulation of the entire PS5 environment.
AnyPS5 is still in its early days, but already has about 76 percent of system libraries and 50 percent GPU shader instructions fully supported, according to its developers. That’s enough to get simple games like Dreaming Sarah to a “playable state” and has led to proof-of-concept footage of the PS5 edition of Dead Cells running as a native PC executable.
We’re still probably a long way off from the day when a solid majority of the PS5 library can be ably run on PC hardware. Still, the recent burst in activity and compatibility progress should give PC players hope that day will be coming eventually.
