articles.title_orig: Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific, sailors rescued alive 18 hours later
articles.title_zh: Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific, sailors rescued alive 18 hours later
articles.content_orig:
A sperm whale cracked the hull of a yacht sailing in the remote South Pacific, forcing four sailors into a day-and-night fight for survival on the high seas.
Crew members on the 52-foot Tai Tam told AFP on Thursday of their weekend encounter with a pod of sperm whales 250 nautical miles north of tiny Norfolk Island.
"There was sort of a loud thud. The whole boat was pushed sideways," said Australian Jemma Cooper, who was thrown from the steering wheel by the force of the blow.
Not knowing at first what had happened, she noticed a brown discoloration in the water and a sperm whale.
"We looked out to our port side, and there were six to eight, a pod, of whales there. So then it became clear that that's what it was," she told AFP.
Her husband Jeremy Cooper said he was sleeping below deck when the impact woke him.
"It was pretty immediately evident it was very serious," he said.
"All the steering gear was smashed on the starboard side, and there was a significant amount of water coming in," Jeremy told AFP.
At 1 p.m. New Zealand time on Saturday — about 30 minutes after the whale collision — they activated an emergency beacon.
"We declared a full mayday," said New Zealand crew member Terry Hetherington, adding they spent the next few hours bailing out as much water as they could.
The Royal New Zealand Air Force flew a P-8A Poseidon patrol plane to the area to establish radio communications and coordinate the rescue, the military said in a news release , which included images of the rescue.
French crew member Martin Jaffre said the whale collision left several gashes in the hull and cracked the fiberglass structure, as well as breaking the steering.
"We could no longer steer the boat, and a boat with no steering quickly becomes a problem," he told AFP.
Jaffre battled to slow the incoming water with anything to hand, including expansion foam, and swam below the boat to inspect the hull, his crewmates said.
The sailors tried to stay aboard as long as possible, struggling to stop the engine getting clogged and bailing by hand.
Late at night, they abandoned the boat and transferred to a life raft in calm seas and under a full moon.
In the early hours of Sunday morning, they cut the tether to the yacht, fearing it might drag them down. Soon after, it slipped beneath the waves.
A 470-foot container ship, the MV Sofrana Surville, rescued the sailors at 6 a.m. on Sunday, the New Zealand military said — about 18 hours after their encounter with the sperm whale.
Even the rescue was scary as the giant ship approached their tiny life raft, recalled Jeremy Cooper.
But within half an hour they had scaled a ladder to join their rescuers, have a cup of coffee and chat with the captain, he said, ruing the end of their Pacific holiday voyage.
"It was wonderful, wonderful, and just a terrible, terrible ending — but luckily no loss of life."
Rescue Coordination Centre Operations Manager Mike Clulow praised the efforts of the rescue team and the yacht's crew.
"This was a well-coordinated and executed rescue," Clulow said. "The crew of the yacht did all the right things, and it was unfortunate to have struck a whale in open water. They were well prepared and the early activation of their EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon) was key to helping get them to safety. It is an excellent reminder that being prepared when going to sea can save your life."
Adult male sperm whales measure between 50 and 60 feet. They are considered a "vulnerable" species by the nonprofit International Union for Conservation of Nature. Sperm whales reproduce once every five to seven years and have experienced significant population decline. The species is under threat from noise pollution, plastic consumption and ship strikes.
The incident in New Zealand marks at least the second time in less than two months that a whale has sunk a boat. In July, a whale that surfaced for air slammed into a New Jersey fire department's boat, sinking the ship with firefighters on board.  Someone on a personal watercraft nearby and a boater helped rescue the firefighters from the water.

Last week, President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. It's their second meeting this year, following the May summit in Beijing. This visit, the stakes were even higher .
We have learned about security incidents from nearly every major AI company, American and Chinese, built on both open and closed models. The leading AI labs are openly debating whether to pace their frontier model development, and the government is working out what role it plays in that decision.
I spent four years as Secretary of Commerce focused intently on America’s economic, technological, and security competition with China—instituting first-of-its-kind export controls on the sale of chips and chipmaking equipment to China to protect our national security, and leading implementation of the CHIPS Act to onshore chip manufacturing. I also created the AI Safety Institute so we could accelerate our AI development responsibly and safely. I have sat across the table from China, and I have an understanding of how they think about AI.
I believe AI companies are right to want to pace the frontier. But we need to stay ahead of China while we pace, because a world where China leads the global AI competition threatens America’s interests.
The challenge is this: We need to outcompete China on the technology itself, while also working with China on addressing the risks posed by AI. Competition and cooperation are often in tension, but the stakes are too high in this case to pick only one.
China has its own reasons to take AI safety seriously. The Chinese Minister of State Security recently said publicly that the greatest risk advanced AI poses to China is the risk it poses to the stability of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Beijing is no more interested in powerful AI systems wreaking socio-political havoc than Washington is; both countries have incentives to align on certain safety standards or even just a shared understanding of AI risks. It is in neither country’s interest for companies to lose control of their AI systems or for AI to be used to create bioweapons by rogue actors. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement of a possible AI dialogue with Chinese counterparts after his meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng is a tangible sign that China sees at least some space for cooperation here.
I would argue that now is the moment to fully establish that dialogue and keep the momentum going. We should do this by convening experts from both countries. I’m well aware that we’d be foolish to trust People's Republic of China (PRC) leaders. But that doesn’t mean we shouldn’t try. It just means we need to develop verification mechanisms to ensure agreements work even in the absence of trust.
Even if we don’t reach agreement on a shared set of standards, starting a dialogue and opening those lines of communication are critical—just as we did in 2008 during the financial crisis, when it was in our mutual benefit to coordinate. And we spent decades during the Cold War in careful, ongoing dialogue with the Soviet Union about nuclear arms control because the risks to both countries were enormous. During that time we developed zero-trust methods to verify arms control agreements even while locked in an adversarial relationship.
None of that changes the need to vigilantly and continuously update our controls as technology changes so China can’t access our most sophisticated compute in ways that threaten our national security. That includes continuously updating our export controls on leading-edge chips, addressing the risks of China accessing controlled compute remotely in data centers around the world, and cracking down on diversion of technology that is controlled.
We also need to tighten remaining gaps in our semiconductor manufacturing equipment controls so China can less capably obtain tools to manufacture powerful chips at scale and service their pre-existing equipment. That work has to happen with our Dutch, Japanese, and German allies and partners who manufacture and service this chipmaking equipment.
Finally, the U.S. government should put a greater burden on the AI companies to take adversarial distillation much more seriously. Distillation —coordinated, industrial-scale efforts by AI labs to train their weaker models on the outputs of frontier models—has become a significant issue in the past year. Anthropic has attributed more than 16 million Claude exchanges to distillation campaigns, and has estimated that over 3 million of these distillation campaigns can be traced back to China’s Moonshot AI  (the company behind China’s version of ChatGPT, Kimi) along with other Chinese AI labs like Alibaba and DeepSeek. Moonshot, for instance, was later caught forwarding user prompts to Claude to answer and feeding those answers back through Kimi.
China has certainly indigenized much of its AI stack, something Xi publicly made a priority in his Made in China 2025 plan, many years before the U.S. government was talking openly about chips or models. And China has made progress on this plan. But it is clear to many that China’s most competitive models, to some degree, are ripping off American ones. American AI labs should be allocating even greater amounts of their money and compute towards finding and exposing this kind of activity so that policymakers—and the public—can adapt accordingly.
The risks and benefits of AI are enormous, something more and more Americans have come to realize as AI advances more quickly than we previously thought possible. There is much to do on AI safety at home, to ensure our society and economy are resilient to the dramatic changes AI will bring. But I also know that safe deployment of AI is only possible if we successfully manage our relationship with China—both by maintaining our technological lead and working towards collaboration.

articles.title_orig: Chinese hackers impersonated an Anthropic exec to get information about AI
articles.title_zh: Chinese hackers impersonated an Anthropic exec to get information about AI
articles.content_orig:
Suspected Chinese hackers impersonated an Anthropic employee and ex-US officials in an espionage campaign aimed at gaining insights into American AI developments, a US cybersecurity firm said Thursday.
The hackers targeted the email accounts of experts in AI export controls and the military applications of AI, among other topics, who work at US universities, think tanks and law firms, according to Silicon Valley-based Proofpoint, which discovered the activity.
Access to those experts’ digital lives could offer Beijing critical insights into how US society is grappling with what many see as an existential issue in AI governance.
Proofpoint did not find evidence of successful breaches of the targeted organizations, but the firm may have only uncovered some of the activity, and Beijing-linked groups are known to keep trying on a target until they get in.
“We are confident that [the hacking group] is a Chinese government-aligned threat actor based on targeting consistently in line with Chinese government interests, observed infrastructure and technical artifacts, and corroboration from industry partners,” Proofpoint staff researcher Mark Kelly told CNN in an email.
Could China win the AI race?
CNN has requested comment from the Chinese Embassy in Washington, DC. Beijing regularly denies US hacking allegations.
News of the hacking attempts, which occurred in February and July, comes as AI continues to be a crucial focal point in US-China relations.
President Donald Trump discussed AI last week at the White House with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, but the meeting did not produce a substantive accord on the technology. Trump has resisted calls for guardrails on advanced AI models out of concern that the US will fall behind China in the race for AI supremacy.
Last month, the Trump administration accused Chinese AI firms of committing “industrial-scale” theft of their American counterparts’ trade secrets to save money and bring the coveted technology to market faster. China denied the allegations.
US allies have also warned about China’s access to AI know-how. Britain’s MI5 intelligence service said Wednesday that British academics have contributed research on AI and cybersecurity to a Chinese institute with close ties to Chinese intelligence. In some cases, the academics may not have been aware of the connection between the institute and Chinese intelligence, the advisory said.
In the activity Proofpoint uncovered, the suspected Chinese operatives impersonated Lynne Parker, who served as a senior tech official in the White House under Trump and President Joe Biden. The hackers sent an email posing as Parker to someone at a US law firm inviting them to participate in an “AI policy advisory committee.” The fake Parker followed up with a malware-laced document purporting to offer more information on the fake committee.
The real Parker told CNN that colleagues started reaching out to her when they received suspicious emails from people claiming to be her.
“My first concern was for the colleagues who might receive the impersonated email,” said Parker, who is now associate vice chancellor emerita at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. “I wanted to warn them but realized that’s very difficult to do when I don’t know who is being targeted.”
“On a personal level, I felt sadness that relationships I’ve built over my career were being exploited by bad actors to deceive others,” Parker said in an email.
The suspected Chinese operatives also, according to Proofpoint, chose to impersonate a senior employee at Anthropic, the American AI firm that has clashed with the Trump administration over guardrails on the technology.
The hackers sent an email on February 26 in the name of the Anthropic employee to an AI policy analyst at a US think tank. The subject line read, “Request for Feedback on Military Integration of Claude,” a reference to one of Anthropic’s AI models. Through the email exchange, the hackers tried to steal the think tanker’s email credentials, according to Proofpoint.
The day after the email, the Trump administration ordered federal agencies and contractors that work with the military to cease business with Anthropic after the firm refused to allow the Pentagon to use its artificial-intelligence technology without restrictions.
Chinese cyber operatives, according to experts who track them, are targeting just about every level of the AI ecosystem, from the semiconductors that power the technology to the people who dedicate their careers to it. US competitiveness in AI may hinge on how well it can protect that ecosystem from infiltration, according to experts.
“Getting AI policy right is essential to our national security and economic competitiveness,” said Parker, the former US tech official who was impersonated. “That includes protecting the people and institutions whose expertise helps inform those decisions.”

articles.title_orig: Democrats rethink their mail-voting strategy as voters grow wary
articles.title_zh: Democrats rethink their mail-voting strategy as voters grow wary
articles.content_orig:
A new NBC News poll reveals that 72 percent of registered Democratic voters now plan to cast their ballots in person, signaling a major shift away from the mail-in voting practices that defined the 2020 election cycle. The survey findings show that the preference for in-person voting among Democrats is split evenly between early voting and Election Day participation. Only 23 percent of Democratic voters report planning to vote by mail, down from 34 percent two years prior and significantly below 2020 levels, while 5 percent remain undecided.
The overall survey of registered voters across the United States demonstrates that 69 percent intend to vote in person, whereas just 21 percent plan to utilize mail-in options. According to historical data from the Pew Research Center's study of validated voters, approximately 46 percent of total voters cast ballots by mail in 2020, which included 58 percent of Democrats and 33 percent of Republicans.
Independent voters are demonstrating a similar trend toward in-person participation. Twenty-eight percent of independents plan to vote early in person—a six-point increase from 2024—while 20 percent plan to vote by mail, down from 28 percent in 2024.
Republican voting patterns have remained stable since 2024. More than half of registered Republicans plan to vote in person on Election Day, while 16 percent plan to submit their ballots by mail. In response to voting procedures, the House of Representatives passed the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, legislation designed to mandate proof of citizenship for mail-in balloting. Senator Eric Schmitt, a Republican from Missouri, proposed an amendment to restrict mail-in voting exclusively to needs-based circumstances, including active military personnel, individuals with illness, and out-of-state travelers during an election cycle.

articles.title_orig: Russia launches massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid, forcing power cuts ahead of winter
articles.title_zh: Russia launches massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid, forcing power cuts ahead of winter
articles.content_orig:
Russia has launched a widely anticipated attack on Ukraine's power grid, hitting key facilities in Kyiv and other major cities across the country, marking one of the biggest energy assaults in months.
Ukrainian officials and national security experts have been warning about the prospect of a Russian air campaign on its energy infrastructure ahead of winter, fearing another extremely difficult cold snap at a time when the country faces an acute air defense shortage.
Seven people were killed in the latest attacks, officials said Wednesday, with state grid power operator Ukrenergo imposing emergency power cuts in Kyiv and three other regions. Freezing temperatures have been forecast at night in Ukraine's capital over the coming days.
"Russia has launched massive strikes on energy infrastructure," Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Wednesday via Telegram.
"Since the summer, there has been practically no day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season," Koretskyi said, according to a translation.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Wednesday that it had delivered a "massive strike" by ground-based high-precision weapons and attack drones at a communication center in Kyiv, as well as Ukraine's energy system facilities and the port infrastructure of Izmail in southwestern part of the Odesa region.
The ministry had said in late August that it was preparing a bombardment of Ukraine's energy infrastructure as part of Russia's response to Ukrainian attacks on its fuel and energy facilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Russian President Vladimir Putin at the United Nations General Assembly last week that Kyiv would make winter deeply painful for Russia if the two sides were unable to agree to an energy truce.
"Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too," Zelenskyy said on Sept. 23.
U.S. President Donald Trump claimed that Russia and Moscow had agreed to halt attacks on energy facilities last month, although both nations swiftly clarified that no formal deal had been finalized.
Trump has also previously urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions continue to prop up U.S. diesel prices .
Earlier this week, NATO condemned Russia's nuclear threats after publicly acknowledging a tense exchange with Moscow.
The Russian Embassy in Belgium had accused the alliance of escalating the situation around Kaliningrad, a small Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania.
The embassy said NATO's "reckless and irresponsible" approach to Kaliningrad heightens the risk of a direct military confrontation.
It added that Moscow was ready to use its entire military arsenal if NATO tried to block the region, according to Russian state news agency Tass.
Matthew Whitaker, the U.S. ambassador to NATO, said that the alliance was prepared for whatever action Russia may take against a NATO country.
"What we have been very clear in communicating back to the Russian side is that we are a defensive alliance. We will defend every inch of NATO territory but at the same time we are not offensive orientated," Whitaker told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Thursday.
"This is, you know, a situation where because of the lack of success on the battlefield in Ukraine, I think Russia is trying to lash out, but ultimately ... we are prepared," he added.

articles.title_orig: Box Office: ‘Verity’ Aims for $35 Million Debut and Anne Hathaway’s Third No. 1 Movie of the Year, ‘Digger’ Could Bomb With $12 Million
articles.title_zh: Box Office: ‘Verity’ Aims for $35 Million Debut and Anne Hathaway’s Third No. 1 Movie of the Year, ‘Digger’ Could Bomb With $12 Million
articles.content_orig:
Senior Film and Media Reporter
Anne Hathaway is returning to a familiar spot — the top of box office charts — as “ Verity ” hits the big screen over the weekend. The adaptation of Colleen Hoover’s bestseller is targeting a solid domestic debut of $30 million to $35 million from 3,510 theaters, which should be enough to register as Hathaway’s third No. 1 opening of the year. She also starred in this summer’s blockbusters “The Devil Wears Prada 2″ and “The Odyssey.”
In a twist that few might have predicted this time last year, “Verity” will tower over Tom Cruise and Alejandro González Iñárritu’s R-rated environmental satire “ Digger ,” which also debuts this weekend. The big-budget film is shaping up to be one of the year’s biggest bombs , with opening weekend projections of $12 million to $15 million from 3,300 North American screens.
“Verity” is the latest of Hoover’s works to get the big-screen treatment following Sony’s 2024 sleeper hit “It Ends With Us,” Paramount’s 2025 drama “Regretting You” and Universal’s 2026 romance “Reminders of Him.” Among her adaptations, “It Ends With Us” landed the biggest debut with $50 million, followed by “Reminders of Him” with $17 million and “Regretting You” with $13.6 million. “It Ends With Us” is the highest-grossing of the trio by far with $350 million globally. Hoover’s film adaptations have modest budgets, making them low-risk bets for studios.
“Verity” was produced for $40 million and will help Amazon MGM rebound after this summer’s “Masters of the Universe,” which flopped with $113 million globally against a $200 million budget. Amazon MGM, a relative newcomer to theatrical, delivered its first major win in the spring with Ryan Gosling’s astronaut drama “Project Hail Mary,” which grossed $684 million globally. Later this year, the studio has “I Play Rocky,” a crowd pleaser about the making of the 1976 Sylvester Stallone classic “Rocky,” and the heist thriller “How to Rob a Bank” with Nicholas Hoult and Pete Davidson.
Hathaway, who also starred in this year’s psychodrama “Mother Mary” and sci-fi thriller “The End of Oak Street,” shares the screen in “Verity” with Dakota Johnson and Josh Hartnett. Directed by Michael Showalter (“The Big Sick”), the movie centers around famed author Verity Crawford, who gets badly injured in a car accident, leaving her husband to hire a struggling writer to complete the remaining books in the popular series. Reviews have been mixed, with Variety’s Guy Lodge calling “Verity” a “listless” and “unintentionally funny tale.”
“Digger” looks to continue a dismal year for Warner Bros. — having fielded such misfires as “The Bride!” and “Supergirl” — and the timing couldn’t be worse. Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. is set to close next week . For Warners, it’s a stark reversal in fortunes from the studio’s 2025 slate, which boasted an unprecedented string of commercial triumphs including “Sinners,” “A Minecraft Movie” and “Weapons.”
“Digger” was greenlit at Warner Bros. for $125 million, but according to four knowledgeable sources, the budget climbed to $160 million to $180 million after production went over schedule. A Warner Bros. spokesperson disputes those figures. Box office experts say a movie of this size would need a debut near $40 million to justify its price tag.
Cruise stars in “Digger” as a wealthy oil tycoon whose company causes a potential catastrophe. Reviews and word-of-mouth have been so negative that Warner Bros. has started to embrace the bad press . In a new ad, the studio told moviegoers to “decide for yourself” after critics bashed the movie as “unpleasant” and “baffling.”
